text:
The first two backlog items, plus the plan they come from. This description is current as of `dad126c`, after three review rounds and the delta review of `7b3a2ee`.

## B01: skeleton, config, CI (closes #1)

- `cmd/sluiceway` with `serve`, `worker`, `migrate`, `version` and `help` (`-h`, `--help`). `serve` answers `/healthz` and shuts down cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM: the first signal drains and exits 0, a second one ends the process at once. `worker` and `migrate` exit non-zero with "not built yet" until their items land.
- **The binary documents itself.** `sluiceway help` lists every `SLUICEWAY_*` variable with its description, its accepted values when it is an enumeration, and its default, and the exit codes (0 success or clean shutdown, 1 configuration refused or command failed, 2 usage error). The variable list is `config.Variables()`. What is held to `config.Load`: the names (by recording what `Load` asks `getenv` for under the full cross product of states of every documented variable), the defaults (compared with what `Load` applies), and the accepted values (`Load` validates against the same slices `Variables` publishes). The descriptions are prose and nothing checks them. The development database URL is described (host, port and database name), never printed.
- **Extra arguments are a usage error**, exit 2, for every command. `sluiceway serve --listen :9090` used to start on `:8080` without a word. The arguments are not echoed, and neither is an unknown command: the first argument can be a pasted database URL as easily as a typo.
- `internal/config` reads `SLUICEWAY_*` from the environment only. Unset or unrecognized `SLUICEWAY_ENV` means production; production refuses to start without `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL`; every problem is reported in one pass.
- **No error echoes a received value, for any variable.** `Load` cannot know which variable a secret was pasted into (a manifest with two entries swapped puts the database URL into `SLUICEWAY_ENV`), so every message names the variable and the accepted values only. The `url.Parse`, `slog`, `net.SplitHostPort` and `strconv` errors all quote their input and are never wrapped.
- `SLUICEWAY_LISTEN_ADDR` must be `host:port` or `:port` with a **numeric port from 0 to 65535**. Service names such as `:http` are refused on purpose: `net.SplitHostPort` alone lets through anything with exactly one colon (a `user:password` pair, a passwordless database URL), which the listener would then look up and quote.
- The host half of the listen address cannot reach the log either. `serve` never returns the `net.OpError`: `listenError` keeps only what cannot carry the address (the `syscall.Errno`, so `errors.Is(err, syscall.EADDRINUSE)` still holds and the log still says "address already in use"; the context error; the `net.DNSError` classification) and names the variable.
- `Config` redacts `DatabaseURL` under `slog` (`LogValue`) and under `%v`, `%+v`, `%s`, `%#v` (`String`, `GoString`), by value and by pointer.
- `internal/appversion`: the release version set by the linker, else `dev-<12 characters of the revision>` with `-dirty` for a modified tree, else `dev`. The parsing is split from `debug.ReadBuildInfo` so it can be table-tested.
- `make check` runs tidy, vet, golangci-lint and `go test -race`. The CI workflow runs the same steps.

## B02: `internal/ids` (closes #2)

- ULIDs, `DeliveryID = blake3(provider, raw_body)`, `RecordID = "rec_" + blake3(provider, external_id, version, tenant)[:32]`, parts joined with `0x1F`.
- **Design change:** an empty part or a part containing `0x1F` returns an error instead of being hashed. Architecture section 5 is updated to match.
- `ids.New` is documented as an identifier, never a secret: `ulid.Make` (oklog/ulid v2.1.2, checked in the source) draws from `math/rand` seeded once from the process start time. Tokens, nonces and OAuth state come from `crypto/rand`.
- `IsRecordID` was removed in round 3: it had no caller on this branch or on the two stacked on it. It comes back with the item that needs it.
- `testdata/golden.json` pins both recipes with 19 vectors. Five `delivery_id` vectors go beyond one BLAKE3 chunk (hash inputs of exactly 1024, 1025, 1031, 8201 and 16393 bytes; body byte `i` is `i mod 251`). Their expected values were computed with the Python `blake3` package (1.0.9), not with this one, and the original 14 were re-verified with it: 0 mismatches. `go test -update` reproduces the Python-written file byte for byte.

## Plan

- `docs/backlog.md`: M0 to M6 cut into B01 to B29 with target dates. Item BNN is issue #NN.
- `CLAUDE.md`: where things are and the per-item working loop.

## Decisions worth a look

- Service-name ports (`:http`) are refused. Nothing here needs them, and accepting them is what let a pasted value reach the log.
- `help extra` and `version extra` are usage errors too, not only the roles. One rule for every command.
- `SLUICEWAY_LOG_LEVEL` takes `debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error` only (any case). Up to `7b3a2ee` it took whatever `slog` parses, including offsets such as `info+2`, which were never documented. The enumerated variables are now validated against the same lists the usage text prints, and an undocumented spelling had no place in that.
- An unknown command is reported without repeating it (`sluiceway: unknown command`, then the usage). It costs a typo its echo, and keeps a pasted URL out of the container log.
- The extra-argument check runs after a command is recognised, so `sluiceway frobnicate x` still says "unknown command", and a later `migrate bootstrap` (b04) can return before the check.
- `config.Variables()` is a new exported function whose only caller is the usage text. It lives in `config` so the documentation sits next to the code it describes.
- Architecture section 8 now lists `internal/appversion`. The README status paragraph is left alone on this branch because `b04-outbox` rewrites it.

## Acceptance

**#1 (B01)**
- [x] `make check` green locally and in CI
- [x] an unset environment means production (`TestLoadUnsetEnvironmentIsProduction`)
- [x] production refuses to start without a database URL (`TestLoadProductionRequiresDatabaseURL`, `TestRunRefusesToStartWithoutConfiguration`)

**#2 (B02)**
- [x] golden tests pass (`TestGolden`, cross-checked against Python `blake3`)
- [x] `("ab","c")` and `("a","bc")` differ (`TestSeparatorKeepsPartBoundaries`)
- [x] the same change under two tenants yields two ids (`TestTenantSaltsTheRecordID`)

## Testing

`make check` is green locally and in CI. Tests that could hang on a regression have deadlines and use `127.0.0.1:0`.

Mutations, each killed and then restored. Rounds 1 and 2 (details in the review threads): raw `url.Parse` error returned; production falling back to the development URL; each old value-echoing message restored; listen address check removed; numeric port check disabled; port range not enforced; `strconv` error wrapped; `serve` returning the raw listen error; errno branch removed; errno branch wrapping the whole error; `LogValue`, `String` printing the real URL.

Round 3:

| Mutation | Killed by |
|---|---|
| one variable removed from `config.Variables()` | `TestVariablesAreExactlyWhatLoadReads`, `TestVariablesStateTheDefaultsLoadApplies`, `TestUsageDocumentsTheConfigurationAndTheExitCodes` |
| documented listen default changed to `:8081` | `TestVariablesStateTheDefaultsLoadApplies` |
| usage built without the variables | `TestUsageDocumentsTheConfigurationAndTheExitCodes` |
| extra-argument check removed for the roles | `TestRunRefusesExtraArguments` (serve, worker, migrate), in 2s, no hang |
| check removed for `version` and `help` | `TestRunRefusesExtraArguments` (version, help, -h, --help) |
| the refusal echoes the arguments | `TestRunRefusesExtraArguments` (every row) |
| `run` returns 1 after a clean shutdown | `TestRunServeExitsZeroAfterACleanShutdown` only |
| `serve` blocks without listening | `TestRunServeExitsZeroAfterACleanShutdown`, fails at its 5s bound, no hang |
| `-h` spelling removed | `TestRunHelp/-h` |
| `Version` override ignored | `TestDescribe` (3 rows), `TestStringUsesTheLinkerVersion` |
| revision cut at 13 | `TestDescribe` (5 rows) |
| `-dirty` suffix dropped | `TestDescribe` (3 rows) |
| `dev` fallback removed | `TestDescribe` (4 rows) |
| `ids.New` on an unlocked shared entropy source | `TestNewIsUniqueAcrossGoroutines` only (data race under `-race`) |
| `DeliveryID` hashing only the first 1017 body bytes | `TestGolden`, the five new vectors only |
| golden file without the multi-chunk vectors | `TestGoldenCoversMultiChunkInputs` |

Delta review of `7b3a2ee` (commit `dad126c`):

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| unknown command echoed with `%q` again | killed by `TestRunNeverPrintsAnUnknownCommand` (all three rows) |
| undocumented variable read only in development with an explicit database URL (the reviewer's A14) | killed by `TestVariablesAreExactlyWhatLoadReads` |
| undocumented variable read only behind four conditions at once (development, level warn, format json set explicitly, non-default listen address) | killed by the same |
| `Load` accepts `logfmt` beside the slice (the reviewer's A12) | killed by `TestVariablesStateTheValuesLoadAccepts` |
| `Load` accepts `yaml` beside the slice | **survives**, and the test comment says why: the unlisted values are a sample, no test can try every string. The tie is by construction, the test holds the construction in place |
| `Variables` lists a value `Load` refuses | killed by `TestVariablesStateTheValuesLoadAccepts` and by the state check in `recordingBases` |
| `Variables` omits a value `Load` accepts | killed by `TestVariablesStateTheValuesLoadAccepts` (the refusal text) |
| level check widened back to `slog`'s own parsing | killed by the same (`info+2`) |
| `Variables` hands out the slices `Load` validates against, not copies | killed by the same, and only that test fails |
| documented development port changed to 5433 | killed by `TestVariablesStateTheDefaultsLoadApplies` |
| `values:` line dropped from the usage; `help` dropped from the commands | both killed by `TestUsageDocumentsTheConfigurationAndTheExitCodes` |

The limit of the recording approach, as the test comment states it: it sees only the paths it drives. It drives every combination of {unset, each accepted value, one refused value} over the documented variables. A read behind a condition that is none of those states (one particular host in the database URL, or a second variable that is itself undocumented) is not seen.

Closes #1
Closes #2

text:
Stacked on #30. GitHub retargets this to `main` when #30 merges.

This description was rewritten after review round 3 and describes the code as it is at `2e6699d` (the fix for the delta review of `edeba03`; behaviour is unchanged since `edeba03`, the additions are tests, comments and documentation). The first submission's text omitted everything the three review rounds added.

## What

- **`internal/store`**: a pgx pool with `search_path` pinned to the `sluiceway` schema, a start-up preflight, and the three ways into the database: `Tx` (no tenant, tenant tables read as empty and refuse writes), `TenantTx` (the only way to do a tenant's work), and `RoleTx` (`SET LOCAL ROLE` for the resolver and worker roles).
- **`internal/tenancy`**: tenant id validation and `Bind` (a transaction-local setting). The context plumbing of the first submission is gone, see Decisions 8.
- **Bootstrap vs migrations**: the application role cannot create roles, so `sluiceway migrate bootstrap` prints a one-time script for an administrator (three roles, `INHERIT FALSE, SET TRUE` grants, the schema owned by the application role). It is a single `DO` statement, so it applies completely or not at all under any client, and it is safe to run again, also as a different administrator. It works for a superuser and for a non-superuser with `CREATEROLE` plus `CREATE` on the database (managed Postgres): that administrator borrows `SET` on `sluiceway` for the one step that needs it and ends with exactly the memberships it started with. It refuses (SQLSTATE 55000, naming the owner) a database where a `sluiceway` schema already exists under another owner. `sluiceway migrate` then runs as the application role, serialized by a session advisory lock.
- **Preflight** (every start of `serve`, `worker`, `migrate`): refuses a `SUPERUSER` or `BYPASSRLS` login or helper role, a server older than Postgres 16, a missing schema (`ErrNotBootstrapped`), a schema the login does not own (`ErrSchemaNotOwned`), and any unsafe helper-role membership. It never counts membership rows (there is one per grantor, and inheritance also arrives through intermediate roles): it asks Postgres the effective question with `pg_has_role`. `USAGE` must be false (not inherited by any path), `SET` must be true, and `MEMBER WITH ADMIN OPTION` must be false, because a login that administers a helper role could grant itself that role `WITH INHERIT TRUE` while running.
- **Migration 1**: the `tenant_id` domain, `current_tenant()`, and `tenants` with RLS enabled and forced.
- **`internal/testdb`**: one Postgres container per test process, a fresh bootstrapped database per test, connected as the application role. `NewRawCluster` gives a test a container of its own when it changes cluster-wide state (role attributes, memberships, who runs the bootstrap). Skips without Docker locally, fails without it in CI.
- **ADR 1** (sqlc, arriving with B04) and **ADR 2** (goose, run as the application role).

## Decisions worth a look

1. `store.Open` **refuses a superuser or BYPASSRLS login in every environment**, including for `migrate`. Under one, RLS silently does not apply and every test still passes (principle 12). There is no superuser path left to test by accident.
2. **Postgres 16 is the minimum**, for `GRANT ... WITH INHERIT FALSE`.
3. A transaction-local setting reads back as `''`, not `NULL`, on a pooled connection after its transaction ends. Policies therefore compare against `current_tenant()`, which maps both to `NULL`, and the `tenant_id` domain makes an empty id unstorable.
4. **No part of `SLUICEWAY_DATABASE_URL` reaches an error or a log, not only the password** (round 3, blocking). pgx quotes user, database, host and port in a connect error, and the server's own message quotes the role and the database. `Open`, `preflight` and `helperStates` keep only a classification, prefixed with the variable name: host name does not resolve, connection refused (the errno survives `errors.Is`), timed out, authentication failed or no such database (with the SQLSTATE, never the server's message), TLS failure, other. The pool connects lazily, so `Tx`, `TenantTx`, `RoleTx` and `Migrate` replace an error that carries the connection target (pgx's `ConnectError`, a `net.OpError`, a `net.DNSError`) and leave every other error, a constraint violation or a failed migration, exactly as the server sent it. **Behaviour change:** preflight refusals now say "the login role" instead of quoting its name, because that name is the user half of the URL. The reviewer did not ask for that last part; it follows from the same rule. **The replacement judges the error, not where it came from** (delta review, kept on purpose): a net error that a transaction function returns is replaced too, along with whatever the function wrapped around it, so a caller's sentinel joined with a `*net.OpError` of its own does not survive. A statement that fails inside the function on a dead connection is returned by the function and does carry the address, and telling the two apart would rest on a pgx side channel where a miss leaks the connection target. Network I/O inside a transaction function is forbidden anyway; the doc comments of `begin`, `Tx`, `TenantTx` and `RoleTx` and architecture section 4 say so, and a test pins it.
5. **A helper-role transaction is cross-tenant for its whole life** (round 3, touches isolation). The first submission's comments said `tenancy.Bind` narrows a transaction inside `RoleTx`. It does not: Postgres ORs permissive policies, so under `sluiceway_worker` with a `USING (true)` policy every tenant stays visible whatever is bound. The comments and **architecture sections 3.2 and 4 are corrected**: claim in one transaction as the worker role, work in a second one as the application role under `TenantTx`. The code enforces it: the transaction `RoleTx` hands out refuses `tenancy.Bind` with `ErrCrossTenantTx`, savepoints included. An item that really wants a role and a tenant in one transaction has to add that on purpose, with a test of what is visible. The B10 backlog line is reworded to match.
6. **10 second connect timeout** unless the URL sets `connect_timeout` to 1 or more. A host that drops packets held `migrate` for 75 seconds with nothing logged. `connect_timeout=0` ("wait forever" in libpq) does **not** lift the bound, deliberately: pgx parses it to the same zero as a missing parameter, and the bounded start is the safe reading. An operator who needs a long wait writes a large number. Stated in the constant's comment and in architecture section 4, pinned by a test row.
7. **The goose session lock is retried every second, 300 times** (same five minute ceiling; one second is the shortest period goose accepts). The default of five seconds made the k-th of N replicas wait about 5(k-1) seconds for a lock that was already free.
8. **Removed as dead code:** `tenancy.NewContext`, `tenancy.FromContext`, `tenancy.ErrNoTenant` and `DB.Ping`. Nothing but their own tests called them, here or on `b04-outbox`. Two ways to carry a tenant with nothing tying them together is a hazard; they come back with the item that needs them (B06 for the context, B25 for `/readyz`, where a ping should go through the same error scrubbing).
9. `Down` sections are not exposed by any command (rolling production back is a restore), but a test runs them, so they stay usable by hand. Recorded in ADR 2.

## Acceptance (#3)

- [x] A query with no tenant bound returns zero rows (and refuses writes)
- [x] Tenant A cannot read or write tenant B's row
- [x] Migrations run and re-run as the non-superuser application role (the test asserts who it is connected as)

## Testing

`make check` green locally at `2e6699d`, integration tests running, not skipped (checked with `-v`: no `SKIP` in `internal/store`). `internal/store` takes about 12 s on a machine that was busy with another suite (20.8 s before round 3, with fewer tests).

Beyond the acceptance tests: binding and role do not leak to the next transaction on the same pooled connection, after a commit, a rollback, a **panic**, a context cancelled before commit and one cancelled while a statement is in flight; four concurrent `Migrate` calls apply each migration once; every unsafe membership state is refused, each case proving it builds the state it names, and the ADMIN OPTION cases proving the application role could really escalate; the bootstrap as a `CREATEROLE` administrator, re-run, and over a foreign schema; `Open` against an unresolvable host, a closed port, a wrong login, a missing database and a blackholed address (RFC 5737, skips with a message if the environment answers instead of dropping); **a database that goes away after `Open`** (a pool opened through an in-process TCP forwarder that is then cut: the call that meets the dead pooled connection, and then `Tx`, `TenantTx`, `RoleTx` and `Migrate` meeting the refused connect, each naming the variable, still matching `syscall.ECONNREFUSED`, and carrying no part of the URL at any depth of the error chain); a net error returned by a transaction function (replaced, by decision, see Decisions 4); `sluiceway migrate` end to end (applies, applies nothing, refuses a superuser, never logs a part of the URL); every `Down` to zero and up again as the application role; `tenancy.Parse` and the `tenant_id` domain fed the same 27 boundary strings (trailing newline, 64 and 65 characters, empty, unicode, the `0x1F` separator, invalid UTF-8) and required to agree; and `TestEveryTableForcesRowLevelSecurity` fails any future table that skips RLS.

Mutations, each restored afterwards:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Delete `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` from the migration (first submission) | six tests fail |
| Domain regex `{1,64}` to `{0,64}` (survived in round 3) | killed: `TestTenantIDDomainRejectsMalformedIDs` and `TestTheGoRuleAndTheDomainAgree` |
| URL parse error wrapped with `%w` (survived in round 3) | killed: `TestOpenNeverEchoesTheURL` |
| Connect errors returned as pgx words them (the code before round 3) | killed: all four cases of `TestOpenConnectFailuresNeverEchoTheURL`, the blackhole test, `TestPreflightRefusalsNeverNameTheLogin` |
| Postgres version check forced off (survived in round 3) | killed: `TestCheckVersion` |
| Connect timeout default removed | killed: `TestPoolConfigSetsAConnectTimeout` |
| `Bind` no longer refuses a `RoleTx` transaction | killed: store test and `tenancy` unit test |
| Savepoint of a `RoleTx` transaction not marked | killed: the savepoint assertion |
| `begin` hand-rolled without the deferred rollback | killed: the panic test. It first made that test **hang** in `pool.Close` until `go test` timed out at 10 minutes, which is a defect in the test: the helper now bounds `Close`, and the mutation fails in 21 s. The two cancellation tests stay green under this mutation, because there the property comes from pgxpool destroying a connection released mid-operation, not from `BeginFunc`. |
| One statement removed from the `Down` section | killed: both assertions of the Down test |
| `migrate` swallows the `Open` error | killed: the refusal and the no-leak command tests |
| `begin` returns `pgx.BeginFunc` without `scrub` (survived in the delta review, M4) | killed: the `Tx`, `TenantTx` and `RoleTx` rows of `TestALostDatabaseNeverEchoesTheURL`, and `TestANetErrorFromTheTransactionFunctionIsReplacedToo` |
| Both `scrub` calls removed from `Migrate` (survived in the delta review, M5) | killed: the `Migrate` row of `TestALostDatabaseNeverEchoesTheURL`. It is the second call that kills it. The first one, on the error path of building the goose provider, cannot be reached: goose v3.28.0 first touches the database in `Up`. Removing that call alone leaves the suite green and no test can change that; it stays as a guard against a goose release that connects earlier, and a comment says so. |
| The connect timeout default applied only when the URL does not mention `connect_timeout` | killed: the `connect_timeout=0` row of `TestPoolConfigSetsAConnectTimeout` |

The two cancellation tests cannot be failed by any mutation of this package: what they pin belongs to pgxpool (a connection released mid-operation is destroyed). Their comments now say so, and that they exist to notice a pgx upgrade that changes it.

The mutations of rounds 1 and 2 are in the replies to those reviews.

Self-review. Security: the classifier prints a SQLSTATE only after checking it is five characters of `0-9A-Z`, so nothing else from the far end of the connection can be printed. Performance: see Decisions 6 and 7. Dead code: Decisions 8. Docs: architecture sections 3.2 and 4, ADR 2, the B10 backlog line, godoc. The README status paragraph is deliberately untouched here, because `b04-outbox` rewrites it.

Not done here: Postgres 16 in the CI matrix (round 3 asked for it; the reviewer ran the suite on 16.15 by hand, green). It touches `ci.yml` and `testdb`, and is left for the maintainer to place.

Closes #3

text:
Stacked on #31, which is stacked on #30. Merge in order (#30, #31, then this); GitHub retargets each to `main` as its base merges.

This description was rewritten after review round 3 and brought up to date after the review of the redesign (commit 24af3f5: decisions 17 and 18, the additions to 13, the measurements marked "review", and the last mutation table). It describes the code as it is now, not as first submitted. Round 3 changed the design of the claim: see decisions 2 to 6, and ADR 10 (`docs/adr/0010-outbox-head-marker.md`), which has the full correctness argument, every interleaving considered, and what was rejected.

## What

- **Migration 2**: the `outbox` table, RLS enabled and forced, the head marker `is_head` with its unique index and CHECK, the generated column `due_at` and the index of due heads the claim walks, a partial index over the unfinished rows of a key, a `prepared_at` column, a 512 byte bound on `ordering_key`, and column grants for the worker role.
- **`internal/outbox`**: `Accept`, `Claim`, `Get`, `MarkPrepared`, `MarkDelivered`, `Fail` (ladder, then dead letter), `MarkDead`, `Replay`, `StrandedKeys` (detection only), the retry `Ladder` as a pure function, and `Cause`, the only form in which a failure is recorded.
- **`internal/store`** (one line, in #31's package but needed by this design): every transaction begins `READ COMMITTED` by name. See decision 17.
- **sqlc** (ADR 1): queries in `internal/outbox/queries.sql`, generated code checked in under `outboxdb/`, unused table structs omitted. `make sqlc` regenerates, `make sqlc-check` fails CI when it is stale. Both run sqlc from its pinned Docker image, so there is nothing to install.

## Decisions worth a look

1. **A claim is a lease with a token, not a held row lock.** The drain spans two transactions and a sink call, so a lock cannot cover it. A dead worker's lease runs out and the row is taken over. Every transition checks the token, so a slow worker coming back after a takeover gets `ErrLeaseLost` and changes nothing.
2. **The head of an ordering key is stored, not computed by the claim** (round 3, ADR 10, architecture 3.2 and 9 updated). The claim used to work out the head of every unfinished key on every poll and throw away all but the batch, so it cost the backlog: see the measurements below. Now each row has `is_head`, true for exactly the earliest unfinished row of its key, and the claim is `WHERE is_head AND due_at <= now() ORDER BY due_at, seq LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` over a partial index `(due_at, seq) WHERE is_head`. `due_at` is a generated column, the later of `next_attempt_at` and `lease_until`, so the index range holds exactly what is claimable: a poll visits neither the rows behind a head, nor heads backing off, nor heads other workers hold.
3. **Safety is the database's, liveness is the writers'.** `UNIQUE (tenant_id, ordering_key) WHERE is_head` allows one head per key, `CHECK (NOT is_head OR state IN ('pending','prepared'))` says a head is unfinished, the claim re-checks `is_head` on the row it has locked, and an unfinished row keeps the marker until it finishes. So two rows of one key are never in flight, whatever a writer does, including one that bypasses this package (its row is not a head, and is refused the marker while the key has one). The writers keep the marker: `Accept` and `Replay` set it when their key has nothing unfinished, and `MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead` hand it to the next row in the same transaction.
4. **`MarkDelivered` and `MarkDead` now take the key's advisory lock too**, before anything else, as `Accept` and `Replay` already did. Without it a promotion can be lost: `Accept` of v2 sees v1 unfinished and stores v2 as a non-head, while the finish of v1 cannot yet see v2 and promotes nothing, and v2 is never delivered. With it, the writers of one key run strictly one after the other. The lock always comes before any row lock, and the claim takes no advisory lock and never waits for a row, so there is no cycle. Cost: finishing a row is three statements instead of one (measured: 0.02 + 0.11 + 0.12 ms), and it waits for an open `Accept` of the same entity.
5. **The claim deliberately has no condition on the state, which differs from what the round 3 brief asked for** (keep re-checking state on the locked row). The CHECK makes every head unfinished on every version of every row, so `is_head` on the locked row already is that re-check. I first kept `state IN (...)` as a belt-and-braces condition, and measuring showed it is harmful: the planner treats `is_head` and the state as independent, expects a fraction of the heads there are, decides a walk of the index would take too long to fill a batch of 100, and ANDs in a bitmap of `outbox_unfinished`, which is every waiting row (100,202 index entries read to return 100 rows). The guard test pins this by checking the plan's shape. It also let the worker role lose its SELECT on `state`.
6. **The claim's defensive `NOT EXISTS` is gone.** It was evaluated on the snapshot, not under the lock, and needed the worker to read `ordering_key` and `lease_until`. The unique index is stronger and holds at every moment. The claim's re-check no longer needs `seq` either: a row that died and was replayed behind a version in flight has lost the marker. One outcome differs from round 2 and is correct: a row that died and was replayed onto a key with nothing else unfinished, all inside a paused claim's window, is leased by that claim, because it is the head at lock time.
7. **`Accept` and `Replay` take the per-key advisory lock before they assign a `seq`** (round 1). `seq` is assigned when the INSERT runs, not when it commits. `LockOrderingKey` is `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(tenant || chr(31) || ordering_key, 0))`, its own statement, held to commit. Two keys whose hashes collide wait for each other, which is harmless. A future transaction that accepts several keys holds several of these locks and should order them, or retry on a deadlock.
8. **A replayed dead letter goes to the BACK of its key's queue** (`seq = DEFAULT`, under the same lock), and like an accepted row it is the head only if its key has nothing unfinished. A replayed v1 is delivered after every version accepted before the replay, and the forward-only supersede chain handles it like any other late arrival of an old version. `prepared_at` outlives the state, so a row that died after it was prepared is replayed as `prepared` and never prepared again.
9. **`delivery_id` is unique per tenant, not globally** (design change, architecture section 5 updated). Two tenants may connect one provider workspace, and reconciliation synthesizes identical deliveries for both.
10. **The worker role reads less than before.** SELECT on `id, seq, tenant_id, is_head, attempts, due_at`, UPDATE on `attempts, lease_until, lease_token`. It cannot read `raw_body`, `lease_token`, a row's state, which entity a row belongs to, or the two times `due_at` is made from, and it cannot write `is_head`: it can lease a head and never make one.
11. **A failure is recorded as an `outbox.Cause`, never as text** (round 3, API change). `Fail(ctx, c, ladder, cause Cause)` and `MarkDead(ctx, c, cause Cause)`. A `Cause` is one of the outbox's own classifications, an HTTP status, and the remote system's error code only if it looks like one (at most 64 bytes of letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.`), otherwise the word "withheld". There is no constructor that takes an error or a message, because the obvious call, `err.Error()` of an HTTP client, quotes the request URL with its query string and API key into a plain column that operators read and backups carry. `dead_reason` is one of two fixed texts. `clip` stays as the last line of defense. Its limit, stated in the godoc: a bare token looks like a code, so this stops accidents, not a caller that passes a secret as the code.
12. **`Claimed` is read-only** (round 3, API change): `ID()`, `Tenant()`, `Attempt()`. A `Claimed` aimed at another tenant already changed nothing (row-level security hides the row). Now it cannot be written outside the package at all.
13. **`ordering_key` is at most 512 bytes** (`MaxOrderingKeyLen`, `ErrBadOrderingKey`, and the same bound as a CHECK). A longer key failed the INSERT or not depending on how well it compressed (the btree tuple limit). B06 should treat `ErrBadOrderingKey` as poison: park it and answer 2xx. The error reports the length, not the key. After the review of the redesign the same sentinel covers a key Postgres cannot store as text at all: a NUL byte or invalid UTF-8, which used to come back as the database's SQLSTATE 22021, indistinguishable from an outage (a NUL is one JSON escape away from any sender). It is refused before the database is asked. `Provider` is a constant of the program and not sender-controlled, so it has no sentinel, and it is refused in words all the same. An id that no row can have (`Get`, `Replay`) is `ErrNotFound`.
14. **A claim leases at most `MaxBatch` = 1000 rows**, documented, and refuses a batch or lease that is not positive.
15. A **dead** row is finished and does not block newer versions of its entity. A row in **backoff** does.
16. Not covered, by design: a holder whose lease has expired may still be talking to the sink while the takeover runs. The token stops it from committing anything, and sink idempotency covers the repeat. The worker (B10) should stop work at lease expiry.
17. **The isolation level is asked for, not inherited** (review of the redesign, should-fix 1). The head marker made it load-bearing: a writer waits for the key's lock and then decides from what it sees, and only under READ COMMITTED does its next statement see what the previous holder committed. With `default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read'` on the database or the role, the snapshot is the transaction's, taken by the `set_config` that binds the tenant, before the wait. `Accept` behind an open finish stores v2 without the marker, a finish behind an open `Accept` promotes nothing, `Replay` does what `Accept` does: `0 heads among 1 unfinished rows`, `Claim` returns nothing forever, no error anywhere. (SERIALIZABLE fails the same interleavings with 40001, which is loud. Safety holds at any level.) `store.begin`, the only place the application opens a transaction, now uses `pgx.TxOptions{IsoLevel: pgx.ReadCommitted}`. The claim needs the same level for its re-check on the locked row. `Migrate` (goose's own DDL transactions, under the session lock) and the preflight (single statements) are not affected, and ADR 10 says why. I chose the explicit level over a preflight refusal: a site that sets REPEATABLE READ as policy can then still run Sluiceway, and nothing depends on a check that runs once per process.
18. **`StrandedKeys(ctx, tenant, limit)` is scoped to a tenant, not cross-tenant** (review note 4, the small part). It finds the one broken state that is silent: a key with unfinished rows and no head. It needs `state` and `ordering_key`, which the worker role deliberately cannot read, and I did not widen its grants. A cross-tenant sweep either calls it per tenant or gets a role of its own: that choice, the sweep and the metric are B25. ADR 10 has the repair statement, and the test runs it as written there. Measured on 4,000,000 rows: 36 ms and 67,631 buffers for a tenant with 99,100 unfinished rows (90,000 of them behind 20 heads), 2 ms for a tenant with 9,100. (`headsBroken`, the whole invariant, took the reviewer 7.7 s on 5,100,000 rows. It stays a test helper.)

## The claim, before and after

Postgres 17.11, default settings, the real `roles.sql` and migrations, run as `sluiceway_worker` the way `RoleTx` runs it and rolled back, 5,000,000 delivered rows present (heap 1.3 GB), 50 tenants, 120 byte bodies, analyzed, the second of two runs. "Before" is the claim of dfc5af4 on the same database. Execution time, then shared buffers hit or read. The scratch container is removed.

| Unfinished rows | Batch | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100,000 over 90,000 keys | 10 | 265 ms, 386,914 | 0.37 ms, 339 |
| same | 100 | 269 ms, 389,626 | 1.4 ms, 2,856 |
| 1,000,000 over 990,000 keys | 10 | 4,142 ms, 4,382,297 (two sequential scans of the heap) | 0.28 ms, 344 |
| same | 100 | 4,147 ms, 4,385,122 | 1.1 ms, 3,060 |
| 1,000,000, all in backoff (a sink outage) | 10 | 391 ms, 237,065, returns nothing | 0.02 ms, 3 |
| the same before any vacuum, after 990,000 heads moved in ONE statement | 10 | 391 ms, 237,065 | 5.9 ms, 3,844 (the first poll after the move: 116 ms, once) |
| 100,000: 20 hot keys of 4,500 versions, and 10,000 keys of one | 10 | 148 ms, 107,234 | 0.22 ms, 285 |
| same | 100 | 152 ms, 109,961 | 1.3 ms, 2,849 |
| same | 1000 | not measured | 11.6 ms, 28,818 |
| same, the hot keys' heads in backoff | 10 | 122 ms, 49,268 | 0.19 ms, 303 |

What is left is almost all the UPDATE: about 25 buffers per leased row, because a lease moves the row in the index of due heads, so every index gets an entry for the new version. Finding the rows costs about one buffer each.

**The honest limit.** The cost is the batch, plus Postgres housekeeping: every lease, retry and finish leaves a dead entry at the front of the index the claim walks. The first poll to pass one marks it, later polls skip it, and the pages that held them stay until a vacuum. The sixth row of the table is 990,000 heads moved by one statement, which no code path does, and no vacuum. **I first gave "about 260 entries per page" as the rate, and that is the best case** (pages filled in index order, 90 percent full). The review measured the realistic pattern, one row at a time with autovacuum off: 200,000 deliveries on 5,100,000 rows took a batch of 10 from 302 buffers and 0.44 ms to 2,511 and 3.9 ms, which is 11 pages per 1,000 deliveries, or one page per about 180 dead entries (each delivery leaves two). I checked it with a run of my own (rows arriving while 30,000 were delivered, a 2 second lease so that both entries land in the range the claim walks): 8.7 pages per 1,000 deliveries, leaf pages 74 percent full, about 230 entries per page. Where every waiting head falls due before any lease does, only one of the two entries is ever walked (3.8 per 1,000, and that is where 260 came from). Linear, no recovery without a vacuum, back to the start at once with one. The reviewer's number is the one to plan with, and ADR 10 and architecture 9 now say so. Under a held snapshot the review measured 50,871 buffers and 10 ms per poll after 50,000 deliveries. A long-running transaction anywhere in the database holds back both the marking and the vacuum. That is true of any queue in Postgres, it was true of the old claim's index too, and it is principle 6 of the architecture again. It is written down in ADR 10 and architecture section 9.

**`Accept` stays O(1)**: at 6,000,000 rows, a 1 KB body takes 0.17 ms and 24 buffers onto a new key, and 0.78 ms and 104 buffers onto a key with 4,500 unfinished versions. The new part is one index-only probe of `outbox_unfinished`, 3 to 4 buffers. (The review measured 0.32 ms and 43 buffers before.)

**The write path as a whole, from the review:** 8 acceptors and 8 workers, 200 keys, 1 KB bodies, accept, claim, deliver on an otherwise empty table: 2,630 deliveries per second at the head against 3,300 at dfc5af4, about 20 percent less. My per statement numbers stand, and that loop number is the one a capacity plan needs (ADR 10, Cost). The review's own table of the claim agrees with the one above within a few percent in buffers. Its times are 2 to 4 times mine at small batches (0.74 ms against 0.28 ms for a batch of 10 at 1,000,000 unfinished, 4.9 ms against 1.1 ms for 100), and its first poll after the bulk move was 360 ms against my 116 ms.

## Acceptance (#4)

- [x] Two concurrent claimers never get the same row: 8 claimers, 120 rows, 5 rounds, under `-race`
- [x] Version 2 of an entity is not claimable while version 1 is in flight (leased, prepared, or in backoff), under every interleaving of Accept, Claim, Replay, the finishing transitions and lease takeover the three review rounds could construct
- [x] A repeated `delivery_id` inserts nothing

## Testing

`make check` green locally, CI green. The interleaving tests are deterministic: no sleep is an assertion. They hold one transaction at a chosen point and poll `pg_locks` until the other one is seen waiting.

**What changed in the existing tests, and why.**
- The two gated claim tests still run under the five planner settings. Their gate row used to be "never due", which the new index walk never reads, so the claim never paused. The gate row is now first in line (due for a year) and row-locked by the test, so every plan reads it first and `SKIP LOCKED` passes over it. It is made due only after the gate's DDL, which needs the table to itself. That the pause is still in the right window is shown by mutation M1 below failing under all five settings.
- `TestAKeyWithAnyLeasedRowIsNotClaimable` pinned the claim's `NOT EXISTS`, which is gone. Its equivalent is `TestAKeyNeverHasTwoHeads`: a second head is refused by the unique index, a row without the marker is inert while the head is in flight and after a takeover, finishing the head promotes it, and a finished row cannot be made a head even in a key that has none.
- `TestAnyCauseCanBeRecorded` passed arbitrary text as the cause, which is no longer possible. Both of its properties are kept: `TestWhateverARemoteSystemSendsTheFailureIsRecordedAndNothingOfItIsStored` (hostile error codes through `Fail`, `Fail` to dead and `MarkDead`, against the database) and `TestClipMakesAnyTextStorable`.
- Two tests took one to two minutes to fail under a mutant. `TestConcurrentClaimersNeverShareARow` now stops at the first row claimed twice (120 s down to 1.7 s). `waitsOn` now fails at once when the operation is waiting for a row or a transaction instead of an advisory lock, which is what two writers of a key do when they get past the key's lock (the unique index serializes them): 60 s down to about 1 s.

**New tests.**
- The lost promotion with two real transactions, from both sides: `TestAFinishWaitsForAnOpenAcceptOfItsKey`, `TestAnAcceptWaitsForAnOpenFinishOfItsKey` (a finishing transaction is held open with the real `markDeliveredIn`), and against a replay, `TestAReplayWaitsForAnOpenFinishOfItsKey`. Each asserts the property (the row is claimable afterwards) and the wait.
- `TestTheMarkerFollowsTheQueue`: one key through every writer (accept, retry, dead, replay onto a key with and without unfinished rows, prepared, delivered), the marker checked after each.
- The invariant as one query, `headsBroken`: every key with unfinished rows has exactly one head, it is the earliest, and no finished row is a head. It holds on every snapshot, so it is checked during the stress test and not only at the end, where it would be vacuous.
- `TestStressOrderingUnderRandomLoad`, kept in the repository: 6 acceptors, 8 workers, 4 keys over 2 tenants, 30 percent of claims dead-lettered with a concurrent replayer, under `-race`, about 1.5 s. It asserts never two rows of a key in flight, claims of a key in `seq` order, every claimed row a head, the invariant while running, and at the end every row delivered. The seed is logged and can be set with `OUTBOX_STRESS_SEED`. A run that stops delivering fails within 20 s. The acceptors are paced to the drain rate on purpose: a promotion can only be lost when the row that finishes is the last unfinished row of its key, so deep queues hide it. Unpaced, the test missed mutation M4 in 6 runs of 6. Paced, it caught it in 4 of 6, in about 0.1 s.
- `TestClaimCostFollowsTheBatchNotTheBacklog`, the permanent guard (in `outboxdb`, so that it runs the generated claim itself): 200,000 delivered rows, 5,000 single keys, 10 hot keys of 2,000 versions, bulk loaded in about 2 s. It runs the claim through `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)` as the worker role and bounds, separately, the buffers of the search (the plan's Limit node) and of the whole statement, for batches of 10, 100 and 1000, with the hot keys' heads backing off, with every head backing off, with every head leased, and after a vacuum. It also requires the search to be one index scan of `outbox_due_heads` and nothing else. Measured: 16, 110 and 1,040 buffers to find 10, 100 and 1000 rows, 21 when nothing is due, 2 after a vacuum. Bounds are about ten times that.
- Should-fix tests: `TestClaimRefusesABatchOrLeaseThatIsNotPositive`, `TestClaimNeverLeasesMoreThanMaxBatch` (1,005 claimable keys), `TestAnErrorIsNotALostLease` (a cancelled context through `Claim`, every transition, `Replay`, `Accept` and `Get`: an error that wraps `context.Canceled`, never `ErrLeaseLost` or `ErrNotFound`, and nothing changed), `TestAClaimedAimedAtAnotherTenantChangesNothing` (a genuine lease with the tenant swapped, where tenant B even has a row of the same entity under the same token), `TestAcceptRefusesAnOrderingKeyItCannotStore` (the boundary in bytes, not runes, the compressible 100,000 byte key that used to pass, and the CHECK), `TestCauseText`, `TestCauseKeepsOnlyWhatLooksLikeACode`, `TestAFinishedRowIsNeverAHead`. The worker grants test now also refuses `ordering_key`, `state`, `next_attempt_at`, `lease_until`, and writing `is_head` or `next_attempt_at`.

**Mutations of round 3**, each run, killed, and restored. `make sqlc-check` confirms the generated code matches the SQL again.

| # | Mutation | Killed by |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | `is_head` judged through a join, so on the snapshot and not on the locked row | `TestClaimRechecksARowReplayedAfterItsSnapshot`, under all five planner settings |
| M3 | the claim ignores `due_at` | 15 tests, including the guard |
| M4 | the finishing transitions take no key lock | the three lost-promotion tests, each reporting "0 heads among 1 unfinished rows", and the stress test in 4 runs of 6 |
| M5 | `Accept` takes no key lock | 6 tests, including the stress test |
| M6 | `MarkDead` promotes nothing | 6 tests, including the stress test |
| M7 | the promotion picks the last row, not the earliest | `TestTheMarkerFollowsTheQueue`, the concurrent FIFO test, the stress test |
| M8 | a replayed row never takes the marker, and always takes it | 5 tests each |
| M9 | the index on heads is not unique | `TestAKeyNeverHasTwoHeads` |
| M10 | the CHECK neutralized | `TestAKeyNeverHasTwoHeads`. It first failed for the wrong reason (the unique index refused, not the CHECK), so the test was sharpened until only the CHECK can be what refuses |
| M11 | worker grants widened (`raw_body`, `ordering_key`, `lease_until`, UPDATE on `is_head`) | `TestTheWorkerRoleNeverReadsAPayload`, each column by name |
| M12 | the old claim, with the grants it needs | the guard, in every phase: 16,694 to 20,948 buffers to find rows (bounds 150 to 10,000), 1,288 to 1,632 when nothing is due (bounds 250 and 30). The bound on the whole statement alone would have let it through at batch 100, which is why the search is bounded on its own |
| M13 | a condition on the state added back to the claim | the guard, by the shape of the plan at batch 1000 (a bitmap AND with `outbox_unfinished`). Its buffers stay inside the bounds on a backlog this small, which is why the shape is checked |
| S1 | the lease guard removed, and the batch guard removed | `TestClaimRefusesABatchOrLeaseThatIsNotPositive` (attempts climb to 3 with no delivery) |
| S2 | the clamp removed | `TestClaimNeverLeasesMoreThanMaxBatch` |
| S3 | every transition error reported as `ErrLeaseLost` | `TestAnErrorIsNotALostLease`, all five transitions |
| S4 | transitions bound to the row's real owner instead of the tenant the `Claimed` names | `TestAClaimedAimedAtAnotherTenantChangesNothing` |
| S5 | the key bound removed in Go, and the CHECK removed | `TestAcceptRefusesAnOrderingKeyItCannotStore`, each |
| S6 | `WithCode` lets anything through | the unit test, and the database test, which then finds the URL and key in `last_error` |
| S7 | `clip` without `ToValidUTF8` | `TestClipMakesAnyTextStorable` |

M2 (the claim's state condition removed) was killed while that condition existed, by a test that had to drop the CHECK to make it matter. The condition and that test are gone: see decision 5.

**Flakiness.** Both outbox packages with `-count=5 -race`, before and after the should-fix commit: green.

**Self-review.** Tests: error paths (cancelled context everywhere), boundaries (512 and 513 bytes, 256 and 257 runes, batch 0 and 5000, lease 0), concurrency. Security: all SQL parameterized, the two sender-influenced inputs bounded (`ordering_key`, the error code), no secret reaches an error or a column, grants narrower than before. Performance: an index behind every WHERE and ORDER BY of the claim, `Accept`'s probe and the promotion (all checked with EXPLAIN at 6,000,000 rows), a LIMIT on the claim, no transaction across network I/O. Dead code: both unused generated structs gone, no unused column, index or grant (`outbox_unfinished` serves `Accept`, `Replay` and the promotion now, no longer the claim). Docs: architecture 3.2 and 9, ADR 10 and its index, the roadmap's decisions table, the backlog log line, godoc on every new exported identifier.

**After the review of the redesign (24af3f5).** New or extended tests:
- The three lost-promotion tests now run on four databases each: the server's default, READ COMMITTED spelled out, and REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE as the database default.
- `TestEveryTransactionIsReadCommittedWhateverTheDefault` in `internal/store`: the default set on the database and on the role, both levels, `Tx`, `TenantTx` and both `RoleTx`.
- `TestAFailedFinishIsNotALostLease`: each of the three statements of a finish made to fail for a reason that is not the lease. The key's lock by cancelling once `pg_locks` shows the finish waiting behind an open `Accept` (no deadline that may or may not fall inside the statement), the state change and the promotion by a throwaway trigger. For `MarkDelivered`, `MarkDead` and `Fail` to dead. It wants a wrapped error that is not `ErrLeaseLost`, unchanged rows, and the same lease working afterwards. `finishIn` is at 100 percent (it was at 75).
- NUL and invalid UTF-8 in the key (six cases, plus three unusual keys that must be accepted), in the provider, and in an id.
- One deterministic test for every row of ADR 10's window table, named next to the row: `TestClaimRechecksARowLeasedAfterItsSnapshot`, `TestClaimRechecksARowGivenABackoffAfterItsSnapshot`, `TestClaimLeasesARowReplayedOntoAnEmptyKeyAfterItsSnapshot` (all under five planner settings) and `TestClaimSkipsARowSomeoneHasLocked`. The stress test's doc comment now says what it cannot see.
- `TestStrandedKeysFindsAKeyWithWorkAndNoHead`, and `StrandedKeys` checked empty after every step of `TestTheMarkerFollowsTheQueue`.

| # | Mutation | Killed by |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | `store.begin` does not ask for an isolation level | the store test (all 16 checks), and the three lost-promotion tests: "0 heads among 1 unfinished rows" under REPEATABLE READ, SQLSTATE 40001 under SERIALIZABLE. Each fails in under 0.1 s |
| R2 | the reviewer's E1, split in three: an error of the lock statement, of the state change, of the promotion, returned as `ErrLeaseLost` | `TestAFailedFinishIsNotALostLease`, the matching sub-case for all three finishers, and nothing else in the suite |
| R3 | `storable` without the NUL check, and without the UTF-8 check | the key test, the provider cases, and `TestAnIDNoRowCanHaveIsNotFound` (`Get` and `Replay`), each on its own, so every call site is pinned |
| R4 | `due_at` judged through a self join (the reviewer's S4) | the two new gated tests under all five planner settings, and neither of the two older gated tests |
| R5 | the claim without `SKIP LOCKED` | `TestClaimSkipsARowSomeoneHasLocked`, by its 5 s deadline |
| R6 | the claim also demands an unchanged `seq`, so it drops what it should lease | `TestClaimLeasesARowReplayedOntoAnEmptyKeyAfterItsSnapshot` only |
| R7 | `StrandedKeys` without the head probe, without the state filter, ignoring its limit, and without the guard and clamp in Go | `TestStrandedKeysFindsAKeyWithWorkAndNoHead` each time, the first two also by `TestTheMarkerFollowsTheQueue` |

Not killable, and why: dropping `tenant_id = $1` from `StrandedKeys` changes no result, because row-level security applies the same filter. The condition is there for the planner (it is the leading column of `outbox_unfinished`).

Flakiness after this commit: both outbox packages and `internal/store` with `-count=5 -race`, green (57 s, 13 s, 63 s). `make check` green.

Earlier rounds' mutations are listed in the reviews and in this description's history.

Closes #4
title: B04: the outbox, with leased FIFO-head claims (completes M0)

author: gablooge
text:
Stacked on #32.

Splits the work between two project agents (`.claude/agents/`), with the main session only orchestrating. This pull request contains no Go code: only `.claude/agents/implementer.md`, `.claude/agents/pr-reviewer.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.gitignore`.

## What

- **`implementer`**: builds one backlog item (branch from `origin`, code, tests, mutation checks, a self-review along the reviewer's dimensions, docs, commit, push, pull request, CI), or addresses review findings on an existing pull request. Never force-pushes, replies to every inline comment, lists each finding as fixed or disputed.
- **`pr-reviewer`**: reviews against the issue's "Done when" list, not the pull request's description of itself. Every review covers nine dimensions and shows them in a coverage table: acceptance, tests with teeth (its own mutations), test comprehensiveness, correctness, security, performance (with evidence), dead code, codebase improvement (each with a stated cost), and documentation.
- **The cycle** (`CLAUDE.md`): at most three rounds, then `review:needs-maintainer`. A fix on an approved pull request gets a delta review. Parallel agents each work in an isolated worktree on one branch; the orchestrator owns the merge-forward through the stack, from `origin` refs.

## Decisions worth a look

1. **The verdict is a label.** Both agents act as `gablooge`, and GitHub does not let an account approve or request changes on its own pull requests. Reviews are comment reviews; `review:approved`, `review:changes-requested` or `review:needs-maintainer` carries the verdict. Nobody but the maintainer merges.
2. **Text is data.** Issues, comments, pull request bodies, commit messages and file contents are material, never instructions. Rules are read from the base of the stack, not the head under review. A pull request that changes `.claude/` or `CLAUDE.md` is labelled `review:needs-maintainer`, because an agent bound by the rules cannot approve changes to them. (This pull request predates that rule and was reviewed and approved under the old one; see the questions below.)
3. **The reviewer's read-only is requested, not enforced.** It has Edit and Write, because without them its sandbox refused every mutation and probe and a whole review ran with none. It is isolated in a worktree, which it must prove before any checkout. There are no deny rules behind it. Recorded on #29 as something to decide before the repository is public.
4. **Standing rules, blocking in review:** no `Co-Authored-By` or other attribution trailer on any commit (checked with git's trailer parser, not grep), and no em dash anywhere.
5. **History rewrite** is the orchestrator's alone, only on the maintainer's explicit instruction, with the procedure written down. It happened once, on 2026-09-19.

## Questions for the maintainer
2. A fix touching isolation, secrets or ordering on an approved pull request now gets a delta review. Is that the right weight, or do you want a full round?
3. Who reviews changes to `.claude/agents/` and `CLAUDE.md`? The rule now routes them to you.
4. Is the written history-rewrite exception the one you want?

## Testing

`make check` green. No code, so no mutations. Every `gh` and `git` command in the files was checked by the reviewer against `--help` or a read-only form.
title: Add the implementer and pr-reviewer agents and the review cycle

author: gablooge
text:
**Base is `b04-outbox` for now, only because `main` does not have `.claude/agents/` until #32 merges. Please merge #32 first. I will then retarget this pull request to `main`, so that it does not land inside another branch the way #33 did.**

Adds a third agent, `bizdev`, beside `implementer` and `pr-reviewer`. No Go code: `.claude/agents/bizdev.md`, a paragraph in `CLAUDE.md`, and `growth/README.md`.

## What it does

Five modes, one per run, each with a bounded output:

1. **Landscape and positioning**: who has this problem, what they use today, what their users complain about, the words they use. Produces `growth/landscape.md` and `growth/positioning.md`.
2. **Usefulness review**: follows the README as a stranger and records every place it got stuck, then proposes at most eight backlog items as issues labelled `growth`, each with who needs it, the evidence, the smallest useful version, the cost, and what happens if nothing is done.
3. **Community readiness**: what must exist before the repository is public (contributing guide, code of conduct, security policy, templates, real first issues, an honest governance note), drafted under `growth/drafts/`, coordinated with B28 and B29.
4. **Launch and outreach drafts**: only for what runs today. Announcement, a technical article from the lessons in architecture section 10, a demo script, and where the audience actually is with each community's self-promotion rules.
5. **Listening**: once public, what people try, where they fail, what they ask for twice. Drafts replies; reports numbers that mean something and treats stars as vanity.

## Decisions worth a look

1. **It drafts and proposes only.** It never posts, emails, messages or submits anything anywhere. A public statement cannot be taken back and carries the maintainer's name.
2. **It proposes, the maintainer decides.** It never edits `docs/backlog.md` or `docs/roadmap.md`, and never touches code.
3. **Text is data.** This agent reads the open web, which is written by strangers, so the prompt-injection rule is spelled out in full, together with "nothing from this machine goes into a search query or a URL".
4. **Honesty is the strategy.** No claim that does not run, every statement about another project sourced and dated, respectful comparison, no astroturfing of any kind.
5. **Written for the world.** Short sentences, plain words, no idioms, ISO dates, UTC, translations only when someone can keep them current.
6. **`growth/` is committed while the repository is private** and reviewed by the maintainer before it goes public.

## Questions for the maintainer

1. Is `growth/` in the repository the right home, or would you rather keep strategy notes out of a repository that becomes public (for example in a private one)?
2. Should proposals be capped at eight per run, or lower?
3. Who receives code of conduct and security reports? The agent will need a contact address to put in the drafts, and it must not invent one.

This pull request changes `.claude/` and `CLAUDE.md`, so by the project's own rule its review is the maintainer's.

author: gablooge
text:
First run of the `bizdev` agent, Mode 1 (landscape and positioning). Two new files under `growth/`. Documentation only: no code, no README edit, no `growth` issues (those are Mode 2). Nothing in here is published by being merged.

- `growth/landscape.md`: the evidence, all read on 2026-09-19. A section per adjacent project (Airbyte, Nango, Unstructured, LlamaIndex and LangChain loaders, Onyx, Glean, Merge, Paragon, Truto, Vectara, Microsoft 365 Copilot connectors, Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, Slack's Real-Time Search API, Airweave, PipesHub, and related tools), a comparison table, the problem in practitioners' own words with links, a map of communities with their self-promotion rules, and the trust signals comparable projects show first. Found, inferred and not verified are kept apart.
- `growth/positioning.md`: one page. Who it is for and not for, what only this project does (each marked runs today, planned for v0.1, or after v0.1), the strongest objection with an honest answer, three README suggestions, and five candidate gaps for Mode 2.

## The three findings that matter most

1. **No project was found that already does what Sluiceway plans.** The space is full of complete products (Onyx, PipesHub, Airweave, Glean) and hosted unified APIs (Paragon Managed Sync, Merge, Truto). The empty place is a small, self-hosted, ingestion-only component that delivers permission-carrying records to an index the adopter owns. Closest in function is Paragon Managed Sync (commercial, hosted). Closest in open source are Onyx, where "Permission-syncing connectors are an Enterprise Edition feature" (https://docs.onyx.app/admins/connectors/overview), and PipesHub (Apache 2.0, a full platform with several data stores, https://github.com/pipeshub-ai/pipeshub-ai). Permission support everywhere is concentrated on file and wiki sources. Chat, mail, tasks and CRM are thin: Bedrock's ACL list has none of the five providers, and Airbyte lists three ACL-capable connectors in total.
2. **Slack's 2025 API terms and the move toward live retrieval are the strongest outside risk.** Since 2025-05-29, commercially distributed apps outside the Slack Marketplace get `conversations.history` at 1 request per minute and 15 objects. Internal customer-built apps keep normal limits (https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2025/05/29/rate-limit-changes-for-non-marketplace-apps/). Slack, Microsoft (federated Copilot connectors), Airweave and Onyx all now offer live per-user search next to, or in place of, indexing. Sluiceway's Slack documentation needs to say which deployments it supports, and the positioning has to name live retrieval as a real alternative.
3. **The pain is real, in public, and matches the design's lessons.** Onyx merged a fix on 2026-09-16 for a Teams standard channel that "was indexed as public" (https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/14840), and has an open pull request about a permission change that is skipped because the content hash did not change (https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/pull/14848). Microsoft's own documentation says change notifications during a pause "are lost" and that apps should resync with delta query (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/change-notifications-lifecycle-events). That last point exposes a gap in our roadmap: M4 plans reconcilers for ClickUp, Slack and HubSpot, but not for Outlook or Teams.

## What could not be verified

- Reddit community rules (the pages could not be fetched) and the MLOps Community rules page (it did not render).
- Onyx's statement that Slack reversed its 2025 restrictions. It was not found in Slack's own changelog.
- Whether a self-hosted Sluiceway counts as an "internal customer-built application" under Slack's terms. This needs the maintainer's own reading.
- Which Airbyte connectors are MIT or ELv2 today, and whether a ClickUp source exists.
- Current coverage of Teams, Outlook, ClickUp and HubSpot by Unstructured, LlamaIndex and LangChain, and whether any emits permission data.
- Whether Airweave or PipesHub carry source ACLs in code for Slack, Teams or Outlook (only their documentation was read).
- Exact provider coverage, prices and self-hosting options of Glean, Merge and Paragon.
- The exact wording of quotations. Pages were read through a tool that summarizes them, so every quotation should be checked at its link before it is used in public.

## Base branch

The base is `chore-bizdev-agent` only until that branch is merged, because `growth/` does not exist on `main` yet. After that merge, this pull request should be retargeted to `main`.
