| S6 | `canonicalPath` uses bare `path.Clean` | the same test: `POST /sub/` answers 404 instead of 418, which is the collateral damage the trailing-slash rule avoids |
| S7 | the unset-base-URL warn removed | `TestAnUnsetPublicBaseURLIsSaidOutLoudAtStart` |
| S8 | that warn demoted to `Debug` | same (the handler is at warn level on purpose) |
| S9 | that warn made unconditional | same, on the configured case |
| S10 | `Header.Values` returns the live slice | `TestAHeaderCannotBeUsedToChangeWhatTheNextCandidateReads` |

Plus 95 million executions of `go test -fuzz FuzzNormalizePublicBaseURL` with no counterexample, after the two it found in the first minute were fixed. The new socket test writes its request line verbatim on a `net.Conn` with a deadline on both halves, because `httptest.NewRequest` cannot pose the question: it hands `net/http` an already-parsed URL.

Coverage after the round: `internal/config` 100%, `internal/provider` 100%, `internal/ingress` 99.2%, `internal/provider/fake` 99.0%.

### Round 3: the mutations on the close-out

| # | Mutation | Test that failed |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | the guard back to `r.URL.Path` | `TestAPathTheMuxWouldCleanIsRefusedAndNeverRedirected`: `/echo/a%2f%2fb` and `/echo/%2e%2e` answer 404 instead of reaching the handler |
| T2 | the slash-less route never registered | `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect`: `307 Location: /sub/` in all four redirect-enabling cases, with the `Location` assertion |
| T3 | the `/{$}` spelling dropped from `subtreeRoot` | the same test, that case only |
| T4 | the `/{name...}` spelling dropped from `subtreeRoot` | the same test, that case only |
| T5 | `coveredBy` ignores an any-method route | the same test: the caller's own `/sub` handler is buried under a 404 |
| T6 | the `escaped == ""` disjunct deleted | the socket test: `POST http://attacker.example HTTP/1.1` panics on `escaped[0]` and the connection closes with no response |
| T7 | the `escaped[0] != '/'` disjunct deleted | the socket test: `POST * HTTP/1.1` answers 400 with an empty body instead of the 404 |
| T8 | `canonicalPath` uses bare `path.Clean` | both socket tests: `POST /sub/` answers 404 instead of 418 |
| T9 | `u.Hostname()` back to `u.Host` | `TestThePublicBaseURLIsNormalizedAndNeverGuessed`: `http://:8080` is accepted |
| T10 | the ASCII host check weakened to `b >= 0xff` | the same test, all three IDN rows |
| T11 | the trailing-colon check deleted | the same test: `http://lawang.example.test:` is accepted |

The socket test now sends its request line verbatim for two shapes an `http.Client` cannot produce: the absolute form with no path (`POST http://attacker.example HTTP/1.1`, which arrives with an empty path and is a 307 to `/` through a bare mux) and the asterisk form (`POST * HTTP/1.1`, which arrives with `"*"` and reaches a handler, contrary to what one might expect).

Coverage after the round: `internal/config` 100%, `internal/provider` 100%, `internal/ingress` **100%**, `internal/provider/fake` 99.0%.

### Round 4: the mutations on the delta

| # | Mutation | Test that failed |
|---|---|---|
| U1 | the whole round 3 implementation (`subtreeRoot` plus `coveredBy`), against the new tables | `a_wildcard_at_the_same_depth_as_a_subtree`, `two_wildcards_at_the_same_depth` and `a_last_segment_that_percent-decodes_to_a_slash`, plus both new refusal cases |
| U2 | `redirects` always false | `TestNoRouteIsEverAnsweredWithARedirect`, eight cases, with the `Location` assertion |
| U3 | `redirects` always true | the same test, five cases: the caller's route is buried or the table is refused |
| U4 | `redirectRoot`'s boundary, `i <= 0` to `i < 0` | the same test (four cases) and `TestAPathTheMuxWouldCleanIsRefusedAndNeverRedirected` |
| U5 | the `Path`/`RawPath` pair in the probe request dropped | `a subtree whose root carries a percent-escape`, that case only |
| U6 | `probe` never learns a guard route | `two spellings of the same subtree` |
| U7 | the `/ingress/` prefix refusal deleted | `a literal under the webhook endpoint` and `a subtree under the webhook endpoint` |
| U8 | the branch that names a guard route in a conflict message deleted | `TestARouteNewCannotServeIsRefusedAtStart`: the message is `net/http`'s, naming a pattern the caller never wrote |

The redirect test drives a real socket for GET as well as POST now, because a routing table is not always one method and the mux's answer depends on it. Coverage after the round: `internal/ingress` **100.0%**, `internal/config` 100%.

### Round 5: the mutations on the second delta

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| V1 | `redirects` drops the upper bound (`>= 300` alone) | **caught**: `a parent the mux refuses rather than redirects` fails twice, `GET /v1` 405 where 404 is wanted and `GET /v1/a` 404 where 405 is wanted |
| V2 | `edgePrefix` loses its `+1`, so the prefix is `/ingress` | **caught**: `paths that only begin like the webhook prefix` fails at `ingress.New`, which refuses `/ingress` |
| V3 | the percent-escape refusal disabled | **caught**: five refusal cases, `/%69ngress/fake`, `/ingres%73/fake`, `/a/%7Bx%7D`, `/a/%2F` and `/a/%zz` |
| V4 | `guarding` never cleared after a guard is added | **SURVIVED**, and equivalent: the name is reassigned immediately before the only calls that can panic while it is read, so the new second-guard test reports `/b/y` either way. Marked at the line, disputed in the reply |

Coverage after the round: `internal/ingress` **100.0%**, `internal/config` 100%. The two cases that used to assert an escaped `Route.Path` was accepted (`/a/%2F` and `/a%2Fb/`) moved from the redirect table into the refusal table, which is the one behaviour this round narrows: a percent-escaped route path went from accepted to refused at start. `ingress.New` has no non-test caller yet, so nothing in the binary changes.

### The nine dimensions, checked before asking for a review

**Tests.** Error paths, boundaries, negative cases and concurrency, not only the happy path: the cap at, one under and one over, with a known and an unknown length; a body with no end; a truncated body over a real TCP connection with `CloseWrite`, because only `net/http`'s own reader notices a `Content-Length` that lies; 32 concurrent deliveries under `-race`, each verifying its own signature inside the hub so a crossed buffer fails rather than passes; a sender that hangs up mid-accept; a hub that returns neither a verdict nor an error. Coverage was read and every gap it showed was closed with a test, not with a `//nolint`.

**Security.** Nothing a sender controls reaches a log, a response or a header: `TestNothingASenderControlsReachesTheLogOrTheResponse` puts one marker in the body, one in a header, one in the query string and one in the path and greps the log buffer and every response header for it. The path segment is used as a map key and nothing else. Header injection through a handshake content type is refused (and the test asserts no `X-Injected` header appears). Every response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, which matters because the handshake path writes a stranger's own challenge back to them. Every limit a sender can push on is bounded: the body, the preallocation, the handshake reply, and the accept's time. There are no secrets in this change: the fake's secret is an argument, never a field, and `Verify` fails closed on a missing one (tested, including the case where the sender computes the HMAC of the empty key themselves). Slow-loris is covered by the server's own timeouts, which now have a test and were previously unasserted.

**Performance.** No query at all, so nothing in a loop and no index to add. The registry is a map read with no lock, which is safe because it is immutable by construction (there is no `Add`). One allocation for the body when a length is announced, bounded by `maxPrealloc`. The handshake request is a struct copy, not a `Clone`. Nothing holds a transaction: this package opens none.

**Dead code.** `Registrar`, `Reconciler` and `MemberSource` are left out rather than stubbed, which is the main thing this dimension asks. No TODO anywhere. `Registry.Keys` is gone in round 1, having had no caller and no item I could name for it; `Entry.Provider` stays and its doc comment names B08. The duplicated `printableASCII` is down to one copy, because the content type allowlist replaced the edge's use of it rather than sharing it. `ingress.New`, `ingress.Route` and `config.PublicBaseURL` are used only by tests today, which is the one honest gap: they are the item's deliverable and B07 wires them into `serve`, and the handler is refused at construction if that wiring ever arrives without a hub. After round 3 there is no exported handler type, no exported route pattern and no `Mount`, because each of them was a way to serve the mux without the guard. `internal/provider/fake` is a package rather than a `_test.go` file because several packages' tests need it; nothing outside a test refers to it and the binary does not link it.

**Docs.** Architecture 3.1, 4, 7, 8 and 11 as listed above; `pool_max_conns` and now `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` in the usage text, which the command prints and which a test holds to what `Load` really reads, accepts and defaults to; doc comments on every exported identifier, saying why and not only what; the README status paragraph says the edge exists, that nothing is stored yet, and (round 1) that `serve` does not mount the route until B07, because a mux 404 and the edge's own 404 are indistinguishable; `docs/backlog.md` ticked with a log line dated 2026-09-20, extended with what round 1 changed.

**What an operator has to know that is new:** one variable, `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`. It is optional, it is documented in the usage text with what leaving it unset costs, and nothing in the shipped binary reads it until B07.

Closes #6
title: B06: Provider interfaces and the ingress edge

author: gablooge
text:
## What

The accept path now has the half that decides **whose data a delivery becomes**. `internal/hub`
turns bytes a stranger sent into one tenant, or into a refusal, and `lawang serve` wires the edge
to it.

The order, which is the security argument:

1. **Delivery keys.** `WebhookSource.DeliveryKeys` reads the provider's own identifiers out of
   unauthenticated bytes. They are held to what a lookup can use here (at most 256 bytes each,
   storable text) rather than trusted to be what a provider package promises, and a delivery with
   no key at all is parked rather than looked up: finding its owner would mean verifying every
   subscription there is, which a stranger can ask for with an empty body.
2. **Candidates** from one indexed probe **per key the delivery carries** (a workspace id, a
   registration id, or both), under `lawang_resolver`, in a transaction that does nothing else and
   **commits before anything is verified**. The candidate set is the union of what they return: a
   subscription may be registered with either key or both, so asking only the query that fits the
   delivery's shape would leave a tenant with a claim on the delivery out of the set. A helper-role
   transaction is cross-tenant for its whole life and `store.RoleTx` refuses a bind, so the
   tenant's own work is a second transaction under `TenantTx`.
3. **Verification, once per candidate**, over the exact raw bytes. Nothing short-circuits on the
   first candidate that verifies: "exactly one" cannot be told from "the first of two" without
   asking them all.
4. **The owner.** None verified is 401 and nothing stored. Exactly one is the tenant. More than
   one is parked, and so is a candidate set larger than the hub will verify (32), because a set
   cut short could hide the second tenant that verifies.
5. **The accept**, `outbox.Accept` bound to that tenant, or `outbox.Park` under the sentinel
   tenant when nobody can be shown to own the delivery.

`serve` opens the database, builds the registry and the hub and serves what `ingress.New` returns.
`newMux()` is gone, `/healthz` is an `ingress.Route`, and no route is behind a mux that answers
redirects. No provider is registered yet (ClickUp is B11), so every `/ingress/{provider}` segment
is still a 404 from the edge.

## Decisions worth a look

All three are recorded in [ADR 11](docs/adr/0011-hub-resolution.md), and open decision 11 in the
roadmap points at it.

**1. The verification secret is a column of the subscription row, not a vault entry.** This looks
like it contradicts "raw tokens never reach a plain table", and I think it does not: `Vault.Fetch`
is keyed by `(tenant, provider)`, and the accept path derives the tenant **from** the secret. Using
the vault would mean fetching every tenant's credential for the provider per delivery. It is also a
different credential: the verification secret proves a delivery came from the provider, and it
authenticates nothing **to** the provider. The API tokens hydration and registration use stay the
vault's (B13). The grant is the narrowest that works: `SELECT` on six columns of one table for
`lawang_resolver`, no write of any kind, nothing on any other table. When B13 lands, encrypting the
column touches the two candidate queries and `hub.candidates`, which is the only code in the
program that reads it: `UpsertSubscription` writes the column and deliberately does not return it,
so `Register` hands back the secret its own caller passed in.

**2. The sentinel tenant is `_parked`, and parking cannot reach a real tenant by construction.**
`outbox.Park` takes **no tenant parameter at all**, so there is no argument for a crafted delivery
to influence. The `tenants` table refuses the id with a CHECK, so no operator credential is ever
issued for it and nobody can be handed every stranger's parked delivery. A parked row is `dead`,
finished and not the head of its key, so the drain can never claim it, and its ordering key is its
own delivery id, so a flood of unattributable deliveries queues behind nothing. Five fixed
`dead_reason` texts (`outbox.ParkReason`), because B25 re-resolves by that column. A parked row
keeps the delivery's own bytes for the reasons a sweep can settle later, and a short note (the
length, and the delivery id the bytes had) for the one it never can: a delivery whose keys the
provider could not read is the park a stranger produces at will, with no credential, and nothing
will read those bytes again.

**3. An accepted delivery is ordered by the subscription it arrived on** (`{provider key}:{sub
id}`). The hub does not parse a delivery and so cannot name an entity: `Parse` runs in the worker,
on verified bytes. The subscription is coarser than one entity, which **keeps** the guarantee that
two versions of one entity are never in flight together, and it costs parallelism: one
subscription's deliveries drain one at a time, which for ClickUp is one queue per workspace per
tenant. Narrowing it later means a provider naming its entity cheaply, and it belongs with B08 and
B11 where there is something to measure.

**4. The candidate set is every row either delivery key could select** (ADR 11, decision 4), added
after round 1 of review. See "What round 1 changed" below: this is where the one cross-tenant
attribution was.

**And the things the issue asked to be decided:**

- **The body.** Copied per candidate, so `Request.Body`'s rule becomes a guarantee. 0.9 us at 8
  KiB against a 200 ms budget, and it is also what keeps a `Verify` that was given up on from
  writing to the same bytes the accept is storing. `provider.Header` is passed straight through,
  and the hub builds no header map of its own.
- **The per-candidate panic.** Recovered, and the delivery is **parked**, not routed: a candidate
  that did not answer cannot be ruled out as the owner. The log line carries the stack and the type
  of the panic value, which is what finds the bug, and never the value itself, which a provider
  could have built out of the body or the secret. A `Verify` that does not return is given up on
  when the accept's context expires, so the sender gets the 503 the contract promises; the
  goroutine is left behind holding its own copy, which is why the copy matters.
- **`ctx.Err() != nil` is retryable.** The hub puts the context's own error in front of anything
  that failed while the context was already done, so SQLSTATE 57014 reaches the edge as a 503 with
  a `Retry-After` rather than a 500.
- **`Registrar` lands**, with `Subscription` and `URLSigner`. `Credential` is declared opaque, the
  way `Hydrated` is, because B13 and B14 decide what a credential holds and a struct written now is
  a shape they would both rewrite. Architecture 7 says so, and says why.
- **Refusing to start.** `hub.New` refuses when a registered provider implements
  `provider.URLSigner` and `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is unset. The usage text for that variable
  changed to say so.

## Where the seam is for B08

**This item ends at a row in the outbox.** Nothing here parses a delivery, hydrates, normalizes,
masks or delivers, and nothing calls a provider's API. What B08 picks up: an `outbox` row with
`raw_body` exactly as it arrived, `provider` set to the registry's own constant, and an ordering
key of `{provider key}:{subscription id}`. The `/v1` operator API is B14's, and it goes to
`ingress.New` as one `Route` per endpoint, never a sub-mux (that reinstates the redirect the guard
exists to close). Parked rows wait for B25's re-resolution sweep, keyed by `dead_reason`.

## Acceptance

- [x] **A forged signature gets 401 and stores nothing.**
      `TestAForgedSignatureIsRefusedAndStoresNothing`, three ways (the wrong secret, no signature
      header, a signature over other bytes), with the workspace registered so the delivery fails on
      its signature alone, and the whole outbox asserted empty as the superuser.
- [x] **An unknown workspace gets 200 and a parked row under the sentinel tenant.**
      `TestAnUnknownWorkspaceIsParkedUnderTheSentinelTenant`, with the delivery correctly signed by
      a tenant that exists, for a workspace it has not connected, so it also proves the keys narrow
      and do not decide.
- [x] **Two tenants whose secrets both verify get a parked row, never a routed one.**
      `TestTwoTenantsWhoseSecretsBothVerifyAreParkedNeverRouted`, and its control,
      `TestTwoTenantsOnOneWorkspaceWithDifferentSecretsRouteToTheOwner`, where sharing a workspace
      with different secrets still delivers to the one that verifies.
- [x] **An identical re-send is a no-op.** `TestAnIdenticalResendIsANoOp` (stored, then two
      duplicates, one row) and `TestAResentUnownedDeliveryParksOnce`.

## Testing

`make check` green locally (tidy, `sqlc diff`, vet, golangci-lint, `go test -race`). 100% statement
coverage in `internal/hub` and `internal/provider`, which is how the unreachable branches were
found, not how the tests were judged: two of them were removed rather than covered (`Register` no
longer re-parses a tenant the transaction is bound to).

**Correction.** That 100% was true when it was written and stopped being true in `1cdc490`, which
the second review measured at **98.9%**: the by-subscription probe's `candidatesFrom` error path
and the 8 KiB stack bound were both uncovered. Both have a test in `75262e6`, and `internal/hub`
is 100.0% again there (`internal/outbox` 95.9%, `internal/provider` 100%).

### Mutations

Twenty-two, one per rule that matters. **Two survived the first run**, and both are worth reading:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `Verify` always returns true | caught |
| an unknown workspace answers 401 instead of parking | caught |
| stop at the first candidate that verifies | caught |
| never report a duplicate | caught |
| do not copy the body per candidate | caught |
| no `recover` around `Verify` | caught |
| no deadline on `Verify` | caught |
| no bound on the candidate set | caught |
| no storable check on a delivery key | caught |
| a delivery with no keys is looked up anyway | caught |
| poison is not parked | caught |
| no URL-signer check in `hub.New` | caught |
| the ordering key is the provider key alone | caught |
| the candidate query ignores the subscription id | caught |
| the candidate query requires one | caught |
| `GRANT SELECT` on all columns to the resolver | caught |
| no CHECK refusing the sentinel as a tenant | caught |
| a parked row is inserted unfinished | caught |
| `Park` accepts no reason | caught |
| no refusal of an empty secret on a candidate row | caught |
| **drop the workspace index** | **survived, then caught** |
| **no refusal of an unusable tenant id on a candidate row** | **survived, then caught** |

The index one is the useful one. The EXPLAIN test accepted any `Index Scan`, and with the index
dropped the planner walks the **primary key** for `ORDER BY id LIMIT 33` and filters, which is an
Index Scan in the plan and a read of the whole table in fact. The test now names the index it
expects and bounds the execution buffers (3 for 50,000 rows, against 500 pages for the table).

The second: refusing a subscription row that could not have come from Lawang was indistinguishable
from letting `tenancy.Bind` refuse the same id one layer down. The test now puts a **second, good
candidate** in the same set, which without the refusal would be routed to and stored. That also
pins the decision: a candidate set holding a row nobody can account for is a resolution that is
refused as a whole, not one with the bad row quietly skipped.

### The nine dimensions, checked before submitting

- **Tests.** Error paths (a database failure at each of the three steps is an error and never a
  verdict, `failure_test.go`), boundaries (a delivery key at exactly the column's bound and one
  byte over, held to the table's own CHECK), negative cases (thirteen `Register` refusals, each
  against a control that is accepted), and the concurrency this path has, which is one goroutine
  per `Verify` under `-race`.
- **Security.** Nothing a sender writes selects a tenant, and there are three tests of exactly that
  (`TestTheKeysNarrowAndTheSecretDecides`, the ambiguity pair, the unknown workspace). Delivery
  keys reach SQL only as parameters and are bounded and storable-checked first, so a NUL byte is a
  parked delivery and not a 500. `lawang_resolver` is granted six columns of one table and no
  write, asserted positively and negatively. `provider.Subscription` redacts its secret in `%v`,
  `%+v`, `%s`, `%#v` and in a log line. `TestTheHubLogsNoSecret` greps a debug-level log of three
  deliveries for the secret, a workspace id, an external id and the body.
- **Performance.** Two transactions per accept, neither held across network I/O, no query in a
  loop. Both candidate lookups are equality probes on a whole index prefix, asserted by name with
  `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on 50,000 rows, with a buffer bound so a plan that reads the table
  fails. Everything a sender controls is bounded: the candidate set (32, and `hub.New` refuses a
  configured bound past 1024, which is already past the 200 ms budget), the delivery keys, and the
  body by the edge.
- **Dead code.** Every branch is reachable and reached; the two that were not are gone. Every park
  reason has a test. No stub, no TODO, no test-only code outside a `_test.go`.
- **Docs.** Architecture 3.1 (what the hub does, and parking), 4 (the resolver's exact grant, the
  secret, refusing to start), 5 (the sentinel dedupes like any tenant, and why a re-registered row
  keeps its id), 7 (what lands when, `URLSigner`, `Subscription`, and the three provider-author
  notes rewritten from "B07 will" to what it does), 8 and 11. ADR 11 plus roadmap decision 11.
  README status paragraph. The usage text for `LAWANG_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, which now says serve
  refuses to start rather than answering 401 forever.

## What round 1 changed

The review found one way a delivery could become the wrong tenant's, and one test that could not
fail. Both are fixed in `1cdc490`, with the argument in the inline replies.

**The candidate lookup was an either/or.** `CandidatesBySubscription` ran only when the delivery
carried no workspace id, and `CandidatesByWorkspace` required `workspace_id = $2`, so a
subscription registered with a registration id and no workspace was invisible to every delivery
that carried a workspace, however exactly that delivery named it. Two tenants whose secrets both
verify, one registered each way, had the delivery **stored for whichever of them the chosen query
happened to ask**, because the hub never learned there was a second claimant. That is acceptance
criterion 3, and it now parks.

Each key the delivery carries now runs its own equality probe on its own index, and the candidate
set is the union, deduplicated by subscription id and re-sorted by it. Each probe filters on the
other key, so a key both sides carry must agree and a key either side left empty says nothing. The
whole table of key shapes is `TestEveryRowTheKeysCouldBelongToIsACandidate`, thirteen cases, every
row in a case holding the same secret so the verdict counts the rows the lookup actually asked.
Two probes rather than one statement with an `OR`, because under the generic plan a single
statement would compare the registration id to the empty string for every delivery that carries
none and read every row that recorded none. Measured on 50,000 rows, as prepared statements under
`force_generic_plan`: `Index Scan using subscriptions_by_workspace`, `shared hit=3`, 0.017 ms, and
`Index Scan using subscriptions_by_external`, `shared hit=3`, 0.020 ms, the second unchanged
whether the delivery carries a workspace or not.

**The plan test explained a copy.** It ran `EXPLAIN` on a SQL literal typed into the test, so
rewriting the checked-in workspace equality into a concatenation left the whole suite green while
the accept path went from 3 buffers to 515 and grew with the table. It now drives the generated
`hubdb` method, finds the statement pgx prepared in `pg_prepared_statements` by the `-- name:`
line sqlc writes into the SQL, and explains that under `plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan`, so
the plan under test has `Index Cond: ((provider = $1) AND (workspace_id = $2))` rather than folded
literals. A fourth assertion, that the probe returned the row it went looking for, closes the one
way the positional `EXECUTE` arguments could go wrong.

**Three smaller ones.** `UpsertSubscription` no longer returns the secret, so ADR 11's
single-reader claim is true as written. A delivery parked as unreadable stores a note of about 100
bytes instead of up to 1 MiB of a stranger's body, because that park is the one no sweep can
re-resolve and the one anyone can produce; `outbox.Park` makes that choice from the reason, so no
later caller can forget it, and the four reasons that keep every byte have a test saying so. The
recovered panic logs its stack.

### Mutations for the fixes

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| restore the either/or lookup (`keys.Subscription != "" && keys.Workspace == ""`) | caught: the reproduction plus three cells of the key-shape table |
| count a row returned by both probes twice (drop the dedupe) | caught: six existing tests plus "both keys on both sides" |
| rewrite the checked-in `workspace_id = @workspace` into a concatenation, as the reviewer did | caught: index name, `Seq Scan` and 1545 buffers, all three assertions |
| `ParkReason.keepsBody()` returns true for every reason | caught: both body tests, in hub and outbox |
| drop `panic_type` and `stack` from the panic log line | caught |

Forward-looking notes from the review were copied to the items that own them: the sentinel quota
question and the stuck-`Verify` counter to #25, the two readers of the secret column and the
constraints on decrypting it to #13, the ordering-key throughput number to #8, and the
caller-supplied id, the secret in the response shape and the refusal list to #14.

## Three things CI found, and none of them was in the hub

This item's tests roughly double the integration-test load, and that shook out two latent races in
the test infrastructure plus one real outage. All three are fixed in commits of their own, so they
can be read separately from the hub itself.

1. **`ANALYZE` racing with autovacuum** (`a3eca2c`). The new plan test writes 50,000 subscriptions
   and analyzes them; a bulk insert that size also makes the autovacuum launcher analyze the table,
   both update the same `pg_class` row, and the loser gets "tuple concurrently updated" (XX000).
   Autovacuum is now off for that table before the rows are written, and the `ANALYZE` retries that
   one error.
2. **`internal/testdb` wrote to cluster-wide catalogues without serializing** (`93354d1`). The same
   XX000, this time inside `testdb.New`. Roles live in `pg_authid` and databases in `pg_database`,
   and both are one table for the whole cluster however many databases the tests take, but only
   `CREATE ROLE` was under the mutex: `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD` and `CREATE DATABASE` were not.
   This is pre-existing and would have started failing for whichever item added enough parallel
   integration tests.
3. **B04's concurrency stress test had a false positive** (`da05a1c`). It failed with "row X
   claimed while Y is still in flight", and the outbox was right: `MarkDelivered` hands the head
   marker to the next version in the same transaction, so the instant it commits another worker may
   legitimately claim that version. The test cleared its own in-flight map *after* that call
   returned, and a goroutine descheduled in between made a correct claim read as a violation. The
   clearing moved before the call, which is sound in the direction that matters (the next version
   is not claimable until this one finishes). I re-ran the mutation the test exists for, taking the
   head-of-key rule out of the claim, and it still fails exactly as before.

One run also failed on a Docker Hub outage pulling `testcontainers/ryuk` ("connection reset by
peer"), which was re-run once as the rules say.

## Review round 2 close-out (`75262e6`)

Approved with five should-fix findings and five notes; this commit addresses them. No behaviour
changes except the two log lines below, and no interface changes.

- **A panic type name can carry the secret.** The reviewer disproved the comment's claim by
  panicking with a `reflect.StructOf` type holding the secret in a struct tag, which `%T` prints.
  A type name is not a compile-time constant, so it is no longer trusted as one: `typeNameForLog`
  logs it only when it is at most 128 bytes and made of the characters an identifier, a package
  path and Go's type punctuation use, and logs `(not a plain type name)` otherwise. Every run-time
  construction that can hold bytes of its own (a struct tag, a struct field name, an interface
  method name) prints a brace and a space, and a func type a parenthesis, all of which are refused.
  It narrows and does not close, because a provider package that panics already holds the secret
  and could log it itself, and the comment says that rather than claiming more.
- **The re-sort had no observable effect** (mutation M15 survived). Fixed at the gap rather than at
  the mutation: the ambiguous-owner park now names the colliding `subscriptions` and `tenants`
  instead of only a count, so an operator has the rows to compare. Both are ids of rows Lawang
  wrote, and the secret, the body and the delivery keys stay out of the line. The sort now decides
  what that line says, and reversing it fails two tests.
- **The two uncovered blocks**, and the coverage claim above, are fixed.
- **Two comments that described behaviour the code does not have**: `newCandidate` now says that a
  row nobody can account for fails the whole resolution (it does not skip the row), and the
  architecture's failure row now names the `dead_reason` it is about, so it no longer reads as
  though a no-owner row keeps no body and cannot be swept. The row above it says explicitly that a
  no-owner or ambiguous row keeps the body as it arrived.
- **The `ParkNoOwner` residual** is copied onto #25 with the reviewer's measurement, and the
  sentence that claimed `ParkUnreadable` is the only park a stranger produces at will is softened
  in `outbox.go`, in ADR 11 and in the architecture table.

### The one note decided here rather than copied

**Two subscriptions of the same tenant that both verify stay parked, and the message now says
what happened.** ADR 11 gains decision 5. The tenant is unambiguous in that case; the subscription
is not, and by decision 3 the subscription IS the ordering key, so choosing one of two rows is
choosing a queue on no evidence. A stable choice is stable only while both rows are: delete the
chosen one and an entity's later versions join the other queue while an earlier version is still
in flight, which is exactly what the outbox exists to prevent. The row is also where the `resource`
B11 hydrates against lives. Routing to both is not an option either, since the outbox dedupes per
tenant and which queue won would be a race. The cost is real and belongs to B11: a ClickUp
registration that writes one row per list, each carrying the workspace id and the one workspace
secret, parks every delivery of that workspace forever. The answer is the registration shape (at
most one row per provider and workspace per tenant), and it is written on #11 and in the ADR. Two
rows of one tenant with *different* secrets resolve correctly today and are untouched.

### Mutations, this commit

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M23 | replace the candidate sort with `slices.Reverse` (the one that survived round 2) | **caught**: both ambiguity tests, ids reported in the wrong order |
| M24 | `typeNameForLog` stops refusing on characters | **caught**: `panic_type="struct { X int \"secret-of-tenant-a\" }"`, the reviewer's own leak, reproduced and then failed |
| M25 | `typeNameForLog` stops refusing on length | **caught**: a 103 byte nested slice type name was logged in full |
| M26 | `typeNameForLog` refuses everything | **caught**: `TestAPanickingVerifyLogsWhereItPanicked` loses `panic_type=string` |
| M27 | drop the 8 KiB stack bound | **caught**: 23,086 bytes logged |
| M28 | keep the LAST 8 KiB of the stack instead of the first | **caught**, after the assertion was strengthened: the first version passed, because a recursing double's frames look the same at both ends, so the test now requires the trace to begin where `debug.Stack` begins |
| M29 | the by-subscription probe ignores `candidatesFrom`'s error | **caught**: only the two new by-subscription subtests fail, which is what proves the new coverage is of that branch |
| M30 | drop `subscriptions` and `tenants` from the ambiguity line | **caught**: both ambiguity tests |
| M31 | restore the old "more than one tenant's secret" message | **caught**: the same-tenant test |

M28 is the one worth reading: the first version of that test passed under the mutation, because
the double recurses and its own frames fill the whole trace, so "the panicking function is named"
is true of either end. The assertion is now about where the trace begins.

### What I checked before submitting

- **Tests.** Every new assertion was proved by a mutation (above). The two tests that cover the
  previously uncovered blocks are negative cases, not happy paths. `internal/hub` is back to 100%.
- **Security.** The two new log fields are a subscription id (the table's primary key, bounded by
  `maxIDLen`) and a tenant id that has been through `tenancy.Parse`; neither is a sender's text.
  The type name check makes the log line strictly less exposed than before. No new input reaches
  SQL, a path or a URL.
- **Performance.** `ownersForLog` runs only on the park path, over at most two candidates.
  `typeNameForLog` runs only on a recovered panic and is bounded at 128 bytes. No query changed.
- **Dead code.** `maxTypeNameInLog`, `refusedTypeName` and `typeNameForLog` each have a caller and
  a test; the two new `export_test.go` constants are test-only by construction.
- **Docs.** ADR 11 (decision 5, the parked-row table, the "produces at will" wording), architecture
  section 11's two rows, `outbox.go`'s `keepsBody`, `hub.park`, `newCandidate`, `crash.kind` and the
  backlog log line for B07.

## Delta review close-out (`bf1b9f4`)

The delta review approved the branch with 0 blocking, 2 should-fix and 5 notes. This commit is the
two should-fix findings and two of the notes. Nothing it touches changes what a delivery resolves
to: it is one test, four doc comments, two documents and one unreachable condition.

**1. The candidate sort survived a weaker mutation than the one round 2 fixed.** Round 2 made
`slices.Reverse` fail. Deleting the statement outright still passed everything, because both
ambiguity tests collide two rows that carry the same workspace, so the single by-workspace probe
returns both and that query is already `ORDER BY id`. The union of two DIFFERENT probes, which is
what the statement exists for, was never observed.
`TestAnAmbiguousParkAcrossTwoProbesNamesTheRowsInIdOrder` registers one row found only by its
registration id and one found only by its workspace, the second holding the higher ULID, with one
shared secret and a delivery carrying both keys. Probe order is then the opposite of id order. It
takes both tests to pin the statement: reversing a two-element union whose probe order is already
reversed gives id order back, so the new test does not catch `slices.Reverse` and the older two do
not catch the deletion.

**2. "Ambiguous" meant "more than one tenant" in four more places.** `5872896` fixed the `hub`
package doc and `tenancy.Sentinel`. `outbox.ParkAmbiguousOwner` and `ingress.Verdict.Parked` still
said it, and a grep found the README's tenant-isolation bullet and architecture principle 2 saying
it too. All four now say "subscription", with the two-tenant and one-tenant cases named and ADR 11
decision 5 cited. This is worth more than a comment usually is for two reasons: B25 is written
from that constant's doc, and `hub.Accept` cites principle 2 by name on the branch that parks two
rows of one tenant, which the principle as written did not cover.

**3. The type-name filter holds for text, and leaks an integer (a note, recorded not fixed).** The
reviewer attacked the enumeration with 13 run-time constructions and every one that carries bytes
was refused. One thing gets through and it is not text: an array length is digits, so
`*[126664548954996]uint8` passes and that number is a secret read base 256, about six bytes per
panic. No digit ban: it needs a provider package that encodes on purpose, which the function's
comment already declines to defend against. The comment now says the promise is "as text" and
names the residual, so the character set does not read as a boundary. Carried to #28, the
provider-authoring guide, which owns how far a provider package is trusted.

**4. `name == ""` in `typeNameForLog` is unreachable, so it is gone.** `%T` is `<nil>` for a nil
value (refused by the character check) and non-empty otherwise. The doc says why it is absent, so
it is not re-added on the intuition that put it there.

**5. ADR 11 decision 5's third bullet is marked as supporting.** Routing to both rows races the
per-tenant dedupe only when the two accepts are in separate transactions; in one transaction it
collapses to the lowest-id pick bullet 1 has already ruled out. The decision does not rest on it,
and the ADR now says which bullets it does rest on.

### Mutations, this commit

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| M29 | the candidate sort DELETED (replaced with a no-op) | **caught**, by the new test only: `subscriptions` and `tenants` both in probe order instead of id order |
| M30 | the candidate sort replaced by `slices.Reverse` | **caught**, by the two older ambiguity tests, as in round 2 |

`make check` green on `bf1b9f4`. Coverage remeasured after removing the unreachable condition:
`internal/hub` 100.0%, `internal/ingress` 100.0%, `internal/outbox` 95.9%.

### Notes carried rather than acted on

- **A caller-supplied subscription id reaches a comma-joined log field.** #14 already carries
  caller-supplied ids as its decision, in three separate notes. The specific point, that
  `maxIDLen` bytes of storable UTF-8 may contain the comma `ownersForLog` joins with or a newline,
  is in the review rather than on the issue; both stdlib slog handlers quote and escape, and the
  writer is an authenticated operator on their own tenant, so there is nothing to forge today.
- **An ambiguous park is visible only as a warn line.** #25 carries the counters for this area
  (the sentinel tenant's quota and age cap, and a counter for a `Verify` that never returns). A
  counter for an ambiguous park belongs with them when metrics land there.

Closes #7
title: B07: The hub

author: gablooge
text:
## What

`internal/pipeline` is step 5 of the drain path (architecture 3.2): it turns one stored delivery
into the records a sink receives. Decisions are in
[ADR 12](https://github.com/gablooge/lawang/blob/b08-pipeline/docs/adr/0012-ledger-supersede-masking.md).

It is **two calls and not one**, because hydration talks to a provider's API and the ledger holds a
transaction, and architecture section 10 forbids doing both at once:

```go
n, err := p.Normalize(ctx, pipeline.Delivery{...})   // parse, hydrate, normalize, gate, seal
err = db.TenantTx(ctx, tenant, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
        out, err := p.Prepare(ctx, tx, tenant, n)     // ledger, supersede, mask
        ...                                           // B10 commits, then delivers
})
```

The caller owns the transaction, so B10 can commit the ledger rows with whatever else it stores for
the row it is draining (step 6). Everything `Prepare` refuses is classified once: an error wrapping
`pipeline.ErrDeadLetter` will not come right on a retry, anything else goes back on the ladder.

New: `migrations/00004_pipeline.sql` (`record_ledger`, `redaction_map`), `internal/pipeline` with
its sqlc package, `provider.Degrader` and `provider.ErrCannotDegrade`, and a degraded path plus two
optional event fields on `internal/provider/fake`.

## Decisions worth a look

**1. A version is ordered under the spelling its provider declares, or not at all.** ADR 4 calls
`version` opaque and, in the same paragraph, makes "monotonic per `external_id`" a promise the
normalizer makes to this stage. It never said what monotonic means for an opaque string, and this
branch has now been wrong about that twice, in the same shape: **it read a property out of the
strings.**

Round 1 killed plain byte order (`"9" > "10"`). Round 2 killed what replaced it, "two versions of
equal length are ordered by their bytes". Its justification was "every encoding whose byte order is
its value order is fixed width", which is true, and the rule needed the converse, which is false: a
fixed width encoding whose byte order is **not** its value order is also always the same length, so
the refusal never saw one. Base64 is the case, and it is the one B13, B16 and B17 run on: its
alphabet puts `z` at 51 and `0` at 52 while ASCII puts `z` at 122 and `0` at 48, so a Graph
`changeKey` ticking from `...z` to `...0` sorts backwards. The reviewer drained the older
`CQAAABYAAABz` after the newer `CQAAABYAAAB0` and the older record took the head and the newer
one's scope, with nothing counted and no error. A hash and a UUID have the same property.

**So the pipeline stops inferring and the provider declares.** `provider.VersionOrder` is a
**required** method of `provider.Provider`, validated once at registration
(`provider.ErrNoVersionOrder`), whose zero value orders nothing. That is the difference from the
optional declaration round 1 rejected: a provider that forgets does not compile, and one that
returns the zero value does not start. `compareVersions` does only what was declared:

1. **`VersionOrderDecimal`**, proved: both versions must be one run of decimal digits, ordered by
   the number they spell, leading zeros counting for nothing. ClickUp's `date_updated` is this, so
   B11 satisfies the contract with its real version field.
2. **`VersionOrderLexical`**, the promise: both versions must be the same number of bytes, ordered
   by their bytes. The width is checked here and a change of width is refused; that the byte order
   is the value order is not checkable by anything and never was. The contract names every encoding
   it must therefore not be declared for: base64, RFC 4648 base32, a UUID, anything mixing case.
3. **`VersionOrderBase64`**, proved: both must decode under the same alphabet to the same width,
   ordered by those bytes. B13, B16 and B17 pass a `changeKey` or an ETag through as it comes.
4. **Anything the declaration cannot read is refused** (`ErrVersionNotComparable`, wrapping
   `ErrDeadLetter`, counted on `Prepared.VersionUnordered`), naming the entity, both versions and
   the declared order. A `Normalized` that did not come from `Normalize` carries the zero value and
   is refused for the whole delivery at the top of `Prepare`.

**Where a provider author meets this** is `provider.Provider.Normalize`, `provider.VersionOrder`
and `record.Record.Version`, which is round 2's should-fix 6 and the same piece of work. All three
name the ordinary shapes that are refused and what to do about them: a dotted version (`"1.9.3"`
against `"1.10.2"`, SharePoint at `"9.0"` then `"10.0"`), an RFC 3339 timestamp that grows a
fractional second, a raw base64 token declared as lexical. Since a sink cannot see how a version is
spelled, re-spelling the provider's own token is always available and is the fix in each case.

**What is NOT closed, stated in ADR 12 rather than discovered later.** A provider author who
declares `VersionOrderLexical` for an encoding that is not in byte order still gets the unsafe
direction, for about half of its pairs. Nothing in this program can close that, because "these
bytes sort the way this encoding's values sort" is a fact about the encoding and not about two
strings, which is exactly why decision 1 now makes a provider state it once. What **is** closed is
the class that hurt twice here: the zero value refuses, decimal and base64 are proved rather than
trusted, and lexical refuses a width that changed.

**2. The A, B, back to A rule, as ADR 4 decision 7 requires.** An incoming record whose id is
already in the ledger, that is not its entity's head, and whose scope differs from the head's, is
**dead-lettered with its own error and counted** (`Prepared.ScopeReturned`), never skipped and never
delivered. The error names the tenant, the provider, the entity and both scopes. The rule also
catches A, B, C, B.

**The count is real since review round 1, and so is everything else on `Prepared`.** `Prepare` used
to return `Prepared{}` beside every error, so no count could survive the refusal that produced it,
and a delivery that died halfway also lost what it had decided about its other records. It now
returns the counters it had reached with `Records` set to nil, on every error path, and the doc
comment says so. The caller rolls the transaction back, so nothing it decided may reach a sink; the
counters are still the truth about what it decided, and B25 adds them to a metric.

Two things about it the review of #43 asked for, and both are tested:

- **The pruned path.** B25 prunes ledger rows that are **not** their entity's head. Once the first
  record is pruned the case becomes an ordinary supersede, which is correct. That also says what
  retention may never prune: a head. `TestAMoveBackWhoseFirstRecordWasPrunedIsAnOrdinarySupersede`.
- **Condition 2 is equivalent to condition 3** and is written out anyway, marked as equivalent at
  the line with the proof. When the incoming record is its entity's head, the head row is this row,
  so the scope comparison is against itself. A mutation of it survives every test in the package,
  and it stays only so that the code can be read against the ADR line by line. Please check that
  reasoning rather than the code.

**3. The chain is per entity, and a ledger row means PREPARED.** Keyed
`(tenant, provider, external_id)`, never per scope. A record that was skipped or held back is **not**
written: writing it would make a later legitimate arrival of that version look already delivered,
and the sink would never get it.

**4. An entity advisory lock, taken in sorted order.** The outbox's per-key FIFO does not cover
every path in (one entity through two subscriptions of one tenant, reconciliation beside the live
feed). Without the lock, two transactions can both read head X and the second can demote what the
first inserted, leaving two records superseding X and one orphaned, with no constraint violated.
The unique index catches the commoner interleaving but not that one.

**5. `record.SealedFor` is asked here and nowhere else**, against the tenant of the outbox row.
A false is a bug or an attack, so it is a dead letter.

**6. `provider.Degrader` carries the degraded-scope rule.** A degraded record derives its scope
from the same inputs, through the same function, as the hydrated one; where the body does not carry
what the scope is made of, `Degrade` returns `ErrCannotDegrade` and the delivery waits for hydration
or dies on the ladder. A guessed scope is never an option. **This is a contract on the provider and
not something the pipeline can enforce**, because it never holds both paths' output for one record.
What it can do is prove it for the fake, which it does twice: directly on the sealed ids, and
through the ledger (the degraded record of an already-prepared version is skipped, which can only
happen if the two ids agree).

**7. Masking.** The placeholder is a **random ULID and not a hash of the value**: a deterministic
token would hand every sink an oracle, since anyone with a guess at an address could compute its
token and confirm the address appears in that tenant's records. Salting does not close it, because
a sink holds every salt there is: the tenant is its own, the kind is in the token's prefix, and the
record id and `meta.delivery` are both on the record. Its 80 random bits come from `crypto/rand`
(`ids.NewUnpredictable`) and not from `ids.New`, whose own doc comment forbids that use. The map lives in `redaction_map`, row-level secured per tenant,
granted to no helper role, sent nowhere. Masking runs **last**, after the ledger, so a record going
nowhere costs nothing. Only `title` and `text` are masked: `author.display` is the provider's
identity of the author, which B23 will join a person to.

Three things about the masker changed in review round 1:

- **The telephone rule is narrow, and asymmetric on purpose.** A miss lets a number reach the sink,
  which is recoverable; an over-reach replaces content with a placeholder, and the sink never sees
  the original while the value sits in `redaction_map`. The first version had only a digit count and
  turned most IPv4 addresses into telephone placeholders (`<ip>`, `<ip>`), and
  a version string, an invoice total and an order reference with them. Without a country code the
  rule now needs exactly three groups, at least one of four digits, and a first group that does not
  read as a year. What it gives up is a real number whose first group is 19xx or 20xx.
- **One delivery may map at most `MaxSecretsPerDelivery` (1,024) distinct values**
  (`ErrTooManySecrets`, a dead letter). The text is sender-controlled through a 1 MiB body, and a
  measured 500 KB of addresses wrote 20,445 permanent rows in a single statement.
- **The masker's pure half is unexported** and reachable from `export_test.go` alone.
  `Find(text).Secrets()` was an exported one-liner returning every address in a record in the clear,
  outside the map, with no tenant and no audit trail.

**8. What differs from the format, and is named rather than discovered.**

- The ledger bounds `external_id` at **2,048 bytes**, where the format bounds it at 1,024
  *characters* (which can be 4,096 bytes, and a btree tuple cannot exceed about 2,700). Refused by
  name as `ErrExternalIDTooLong` rather than as "index row size exceeds maximum". If a provider ever
  mints one that long, the format's own limit should become a byte limit in a v2.
- A title or text that **masking** makes longer than the format allows is a dead letter
  (`ErrMaskedTooLong`). Cutting it down again loses content silently and leaving it unmasked is the
  one thing this stage must not do. A placeholder is 34 characters replacing something between 6 and
  21, so this is a whole class and not only "a title cut to exactly the limit": any field more than
  roughly 62% short secrets by length dies here, whatever its size. Realistic content is nowhere
  near that.
- A version this stage cannot order against the entity's head is a dead letter
  (`ErrVersionNotComparable`), which the format does not contemplate at all: it calls `version`
  opaque. Decision 1 above says why refusing beats guessing.

**Docs changed in this branch:** architecture 3.2 (steps 4, 5 and 7, and the two-call shape),
section 5 (what forward-only is decided by, and what the ledger holds), section 7 (`Degrader`, what
lands when, the masking row), ADR 12, the ADR index, the roadmap's open-decisions table, the README
status paragraph, and the backlog tick and log line.

## Acceptance

- [x] **An old version arriving after a newer one never gets a `supersedes` pointing at the newer.**
  Both shapes are tested. `TestAnOldVersionArrivingAfterANewerOneNeverSupersedesIt` (the old version
  was prepared before: it is skipped, and its ledger row still supersedes nothing, so no link was
  ever repointed) and `TestAnOlderVersionNeverSeenBeforeIsHeldBack` (a replayed dead letter the
  ledger has never seen: held back, counted, and not written to the ledger).
  `TestTwoWritersOfOneEntityLeaveOneChain` walks the links and proves the whole chain is one path.
  The version order itself is tested in **both** directions and under **every declared spelling**,
  which is what makes this line true for an unpadded counter and for a base64 changeKey:
  `TestTheVersionOrderWorksInBothDirections` (padded, unpadded forward, unpadded backward),
  `TestAReplayedDeadLetterNeverTakesTheHeadOrItsScope` (round 1's reproduction, asserting the head
  **and its scope** are unchanged), `TestABase64CounterIsOrderedByWhatItDecodesTo` (round 2's
  reproduction, both directions so that a stage answering "stale" to everything cannot pass),
  `TestTwoVersionsThatCannotBeOrderedAreRefused`,
  `TestADeliveryWhoseProviderDeclaresNoVersionOrderIsRefused`,
  `TestNewRegistryRefusesAProviderWithNoVersionOrder`, and
  `TestTheVersionOrderIsTheDeclaredOrderAndNothingElse` (31 pairs across the four orders, each
  checked both ways round for antisymmetry, with the same pair appearing under two declarations
  where that is what shows the declaration doing the work).
- [x] **Masked text contains no email, phone or IBAN from the fixture set.**
  `TestMaskedTextHoldsNoSecretFromTheFixtureSet`, and `TestTheMaskerRunsOnWhatLeavesTheStage` for a
  record the pipeline is about to hand to a sink.
- [x] **A ledgered id is skipped.** `TestALedgeredIDIsSkipped`.

## Testing

`make check` green. Coverage after round 2: `internal/pipeline` 96.0%, `internal/provider` 92.1%,
`internal/provider/fake` 96.9%, `internal/store` 89.9%, `internal/ids` 84.6%. What is uncovered in
the pipeline is the "the database did not answer" wrapper on four calls, plus the entropy source
failing inside `token`; one of the four is reached by
`TestADatabaseThatCannotBeReachedIsNotADeadLetter` (a context that is already done), and the rest
would need fault injection into pgx or into `crypto/rand`. Round 1 added one that does not:
revoking INSERT on `redaction_map` reaches the masker's error path through the real statement.

**The fixture set is adversarial, not convenient.** An address inside a URL and inside a display
name, a number with separators and with an international prefix, an IBAN with and without spaces,
and for every pattern cases that must **not** match: a handle, a domain with no dot, a one-letter
top level domain, an epoch in milliseconds, five IPv4 addresses, a date, a Slack timestamp, an
order id, a version string, a hash, two timestamps, an invoice total, and an IBAN whose check digits
are wrong. (The IPv4 addresses and the four classes after them came out of review round 1, where
most of them were being masked as telephone numbers.) `TestTheIBANRuleIsTheChecksumAndNotTheShape` pairs two strings that
differ in nothing but their check digits, which is what says the mod-97 check is doing the work.
`TestTheMaskerLeavesOrdinaryTextExactlyAsItIs` is what a masker returning a constant fails.

### Mutations

Twenty-four, one at a time, each restored afterwards. Killers named where it is not obvious.

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The ledger never reports a known id | killed (6 tests) |
| 2 | The move-back condition never fires | killed |
| 3 | The forward-only check never fires | killed |
| 4 | `Supersedes` is never set on the record | killed (4 tests) |
| 5 | The chain is keyed per scope (scope added to the head lookup) | killed (8 tests) |
| 6 | The old head is never demoted | killed (10 tests) |
| 7 | No entity advisory lock | killed, 5 runs out of 5 |
| 8 | The `SealedFor` check is removed | killed |
| 9 | The automation gate never drops | killed |
| 9b | The automation gate ignores its option | killed |
| 10 | `meta.delivery` is not set | killed |
| 10b | No external id byte bound | killed |
| 11 | **Masking moved before the ledger** | **SURVIVED at first.** See below. |
| 12 | The IBAN checksum always passes | killed (4 tests) |
| 13 | **The phone digit count always passes** | **SURVIVED the end-to-end tests at first.** See below. |
| 14 | No boundary rule on a match | killed |
| 14b | No bound on the length of a matched value | killed |
| 15 | No length check after masking | killed |
| 16 | A missing token leaves the value in place | killed |
| 17 | One token per kind instead of per value | killed (3 tests) |
| 18 | The degraded path guesses a container | killed (both packages) |
| 19 | The degraded path builds its own scope | killed (both packages) |
| 20 | `ErrCannotDegrade` is treated as a dead letter | killed |
| 21 | **Entity locks are not sorted** | **SURVIVED.** See below. |
| 22 | Condition 2 of ADR 4 decision 7 never fires | **survives, and is equivalent.** Proof in ADR 12 and at the line. |
| 23 | The version comparison is reversed | killed |
| 24 | A one-letter top level domain is an email | killed |

**Mutation 11 survived and the test was fixed.** Masking before the ledger instead of after was
invisible, because one value is one row in the map however often the masker runs: the row count does
not move. `TestASkippedRecordIsNotMasked` now compares `last_seen_at` as well, which the upsert
writes on every visit, and the mutant dies.

**Mutation 13 survived the end-to-end tests and the test was fixed.** Every "must not match" phone
fixture was already refused by the pattern a step earlier, so the digit count had no evidence
outside its own unit test. Three fixtures the pattern accepts and the count rejects (`+4420794`,
`+4420794609581234`, `1234 5678 9012 3456`) were added, and the mutant now dies twice.

**Mutation 21 survived and the code was changed.** Nothing pinned the order the entity locks are
taken in, which is the whole defence against two deliveries of the same entities deadlocking. The
ordering is now `entityKeys`, a function of its own, with `TestEntityLocksAreTakenInOneOrder` on it.
It asserts the order rather than the absence of a deadlock, because a deadlock needs an interleaving
no test can ask for: a test that ran two opposite deliveries and saw no error would pass just as
happily with the sorting gone.

**Mutation 22 survives and is equivalent**, with the proof written at the line and in ADR 12. It is
condition 2 of ADR 4 decision 7 ("not the head"), which cannot change an answer because condition 3
compares a scope with itself when the incoming record is the head. It stays for readability against
the ADR. This is the one live-looking mutant in the change and it is the thing to argue with.

### The self-review

- **Tests.** Error paths (every named refusal has a test, and one proves a database that is not
  answering is *not* a dead letter), boundaries (the exact character where masking outgrows a field,
  the byte where an external id stops fitting a chain key), negative cases (fifteen strings that
  look like secrets and are not), concurrency (six racing moves of one entity, chain walked link by
  link).
- **Security.** Nothing a sender controls is unbounded: a masked value is capped at 512 bytes, an
  external id at 2,048, and every regular expression is RE2 so none can be made to run long. The
  server's **message and detail** from the redaction upsert are not passed on, because a failed
  insert can quote the value it tried to store, which is the very thing being masked; since round 1
  the **SQLSTATE and the constraint name** are, because neither can hold a value and without them a
  deadline, a lost connection, an RLS refusal and a CHECK violation read alike. No SQL is built by
  string concatenation. `redaction_map` and `record_ledger` are row-level secured and forced, and
  **no helper role is granted anything on either**, which since round 1 is pinned by
  `TestHelperRolesHoldOnlyTheGrantsTheDesignNames` in `internal/store` rather than merely being
  true: it lists the whole privilege surface of both helper roles over every table and fails on
  anything not on a three-entry allowlist.

  **Correction from round 1:** an earlier version of this description said the ledger's insert being
  refused by RLS is "the second lock on the door behind `SealedFor`". That is only true when the
  `tenant` argument and the transaction's binding disagree, which no test covers. For the case the
  tests do cover, a record sealed for A delivered under B with both `tx` and `tenant` being B, there
  is no second lock: `SealedFor` is the only thing standing there, which makes it more important
  than that sentence implied, not less.
- **Performance.** No query in a loop: one statement per entity for the lock, two reads and at most
  two writes per record, and **one** statement for the whole delivery's redaction mappings however
  many values it found. Every WHERE is an equality probe on a whole index prefix
  (`record_ledger_one_head` for the head and the demote, the primary key for the id lookup, the
  unique constraint for the upsert), and the head index holds only heads, so it is the size of the
  entity count and not of the ledger. No transaction is held across network I/O: that is the whole
  reason `Normalize` and `Prepare` are separate calls.
- **Dead code.** No stub and no TODO. `Normalized.Records()` was removed from the public API when it
  turned out only tests wanted it, and it lives in `export_test.go` instead, with `ValidIBAN`,
  `ValidPhone`, `EntityKeys` and `NormalizedFor`, which are all there for tests of rules the
  production path cannot reach on demand. `redaction_map.last_seen_at` is written by the upsert's
  conflict path (which has to write something to return the row), is what an operator prunes the map
  by, and is now what one test asserts on.
- **Docs.** Listed above. Everything an operator has to know is in ADR 12: what a dead letter of this
  kind means and what they do about it (ADR 4 has the procedure), what retention may and may not
  prune, and that `redaction_map` holds personal data.

### What is left for later items, on purpose

- **The outbox row itself.** This stage classifies and counts; B10 writes the dead letter, walks the
  ladder and adds the `outbox.Cause` classes for it. Adding those classes here would have left them
  unused.
- **The metric.** ADR 4 asks for the A, B, A case to be counted. It is counted, on
  `Prepared.ScopeReturned`, which survives the error that carries it; B25 is the item that has a
  Prometheus registry to put it in. (In the first version of this branch the count did not exist
  anywhere, while this line, ADR 12 and the backlog all said it did. Round 1 caught that.)
- **Re-draining a `prepared` row.** Architecture 3.2 step 7 now says it: such a row is delivered
  from what step 6 stored and is not prepared again, because its ids are in the ledger and
  re-deriving them would skip every one. The store for that belongs to B10, which owns the crash
  test.
